nodes.name: Finite q-Pochhammer symbol, q-factorial and Gaussian binomial coefficient
nodes.statement: Define the \emph{finite} $q$-Pochhammer symbol \[ (a; q)_n = \prod_{k=0}^{n-1} (1 - a q^k), \qquad (a; q)_0 = 1, \] the \emph{$q$-factorial} $[n]_q! = (q;q)_n / (1-q)^n$, and the \emph{Gaussian binomial coefficient} \[ \binom{n}{k}_q = \frac{(q; q)_n}{(q; q)_k \, (q; q)_{n-k}} \qquad (0 \leq k \leq n). \] By convention $\binom{n}{k}_q = 0$ for $k < 0$ or $k > n$.
nodes.statement_short: Defines $(a;q)_n$, $[n]_q!$ and $\binom{n}{k}_q$ as quotient of q-Pochhammer symbols (zero outside $0\le k\le n$).

nodes.name: Finite q-binomial theorem
nodes.statement: In $\mathbb{Z}[q, z]$, for every $n \geq 0$, \[ \prod_{k=0}^{n-1} (1 + z q^k) = \sum_{k=0}^n q^{\binom{k}{2}} \binom{n}{k}_q z^k. \]
nodes.label: thm:qbin-finite

nodes.name: Cauchy identity (infinite q-binomial theorem)
nodes.statement: For $|q| < 1$ and any $a, z \in \mathbb{C}$ with $|z| < 1$, \[ \sum_{n=0}^\infty \frac{(a; q)_n}{(q; q)_n} z^n = \frac{(a z; q)_\infty}{(z; q)_\infty}. \]
conclusions: \sum_{n=0}^\infty \frac{(a; q)_n}{(q; q)_n} z^n = \frac{(a z; q)_\infty}{(z; q)_\infty}.
also_stated_at: For $a, z, q \in \mathbb{C}$ with $\|q\| < 1$ and $\|z\| < 1$, \[ \sum_{n=0}^{\infty} \frac{(a; q)_n}{(q; q)_n}\, z^n = \frac{(a z; q)_\infty}{(z; q)_\infty}. \] (Equivalent to Theorem~\ref{thm:qbin-infinite}.) The Lean theorem is \texttt{QSeries.hasSum\_qPochhammer\_div\_mul\_pow} in \texttt{QSeries/CauchyIdentity.lean} (in \texttt{Qseries\_Aristotle\_new}). The proof realised in Lean follows Heine's functional-equation argument spelled out in the proof of Theorem~\ref{thm:qbin-infinite} above, organised under \texttt{section CauchyIdentity}: non-vanishing of $(z;q)_\infty$ (\texttt{qPochhammerInf\_z\_q\_ne\_zero}), the telescoping recursion $(z;q)_\infty = (1-z)\,(zq;q)_\infty$ (\texttt{qPochhammerInf\_recursion}), the coefficient recurrence $c_{n+1}(1-q^{n+1}) = c_n(1 - a q^n)$ (\texttt{cauchyCoeff\_succ\_mul}), the functional equations for $F$ and $G$ (\texttt{cauchy\_functional\_eq\_F}, \texttt{cauchy\_functional\_eq\_G}), iteration on the disc (\texttt{iterated\_functional\_eq\_disc}), and the Tannery-based limit $F(q^n z) \to 1$ (\texttt{tendsto\_F\_qpow}). The alternative route via a finite Cauchy-type analog of Theorem~\ref{thm:qbin-finite} is not formalised.
nodes.label: thm:qbin-infinite

nodes.name: Euler identities as specializations of the Cauchy identity
nodes.statement: The two Euler identities follow from Theorem~\ref{thm:qbin-infinite} by specializing $a = 0$ (gives $1/(z;q)_\infty = \sum z^n / (q;q)_n$) and by sending $a \to \infty$ along $a = -y/q^N$ with $N \to \infty$, then renaming (gives $(-z;q)_\infty = \sum q^{\binom{n}{2}} z^n / (q;q)_n$).
nodes.statement_short: Both Euler identities follow from the Cauchy identity by $a=0$ and by $a\to\infty$ with renaming.

nodes.name: q-Pascal identity
nodes.statement: For all $n, k \in \mathbb{N}$, \[ \binom{n+1}{k+1}_q \;=\; \binom{n}{k+1}_q + q^{n - k}\,\binom{n}{k}_q. \] (Equivalently, with $k \geq 1$: $\binom{n+1}{k}_q = \binom{n}{k}_q + q^{n - k + 1}\binom{n}{k-1}_q$. A symmetric form $\binom{n+1}{k+1}_q = q^{k+1}\binom{n}{k+1}_q + \binom{n}{k}_q$ also holds; we use the first.)
nodes.label: lem:qpascal

nodes.name: Proof of q-Pascal identity
nodes.statement: This is the recursive defining equation of $\binom{n}{k}_q$ in Definition~\ref{def:qBinom}, hence \texttt{rfl} in Lean. Equivalently, by direct computation from the quotient form $\binom{n}{k}_q = (q;q)_n / \bigl((q;q)_k(q;q)_{n-k}\bigr)$ (valid when $k \leq n$ and the denominators are nonzero): $\binom{n}{k}_q + q^{n-k+1}\binom{n}{k-1}_q = \binom{n}{k-1}_q \cdot \tfrac{(1 - q^{n-k+1}) + q^{n-k+1}(1 - q^k)}{1 - q^k} = \binom{n}{k-1}_q \cdot \tfrac{1 - q^{n+1}}{1 - q^k} = \binom{n+1}{k}_q$, recovering the off-by-one form.
nodes.statement_short: Holds by the recursive definition (rfl); alternatively direct computation from the quotient form.

nodes.name: Proof of the finite q-binomial theorem
nodes.statement: Induction on $n$, following the Lean proof \texttt{QSeries.prod\_one\_add\_mul\_pow\_eq\_sum\_qBinom} in \texttt{QSeries/FiniteBinomial.lean}. The case $n = 0$ gives $1 = 1$. For the inductive step, set $P_n(z) := \prod_{k=0}^{n-1}(1 + z q^k)$ and $Q_n(z) := \sum_{k=0}^{n} q^{\binom{k}{2}}\binom{n}{k}_q z^k$, so the theorem reads $P_n = Q_n$. By \texttt{Finset.prod\_range\_succ} and the inductive hypothesis $P_n = Q_n$, \[ P_{n+1}(z) \;=\; P_n(z)\,(1 + z q^n) \;=\; Q_n(z)\,(1 + z q^n), \] so it suffices to show $Q_{n+1}(z) = Q_n(z)\,(1 + z q^n)$. We decompose $Q_{n+1}(z) = \sum_{k=0}^{n+1} q^{\binom{k}{2}}\binom{n+1}{k}_q z^k$ in four explicit steps (mirroring \texttt{stepB}--\texttt{stepD} of the Lean proof). \emph{Step A (peel off $k = 0$ via \texttt{Finset.sum\_range\_succ'}).} Using $\binom{n+1}{0}_q = 1$, \[ Q_{n+1}(z) \;=\; 1 \;+\; \sum_{k=0}^{n} q^{\binom{k+1}{2}}\,\binom{n+1}{k+1}_q\,z^{k+1}. \] \emph{Step B ($q$-Pascal split).} Apply Lemma~\ref{lem:qpascal} inside the sum and split via \texttt{Finset.sum\_add\_distrib}: \[ \sum_{k=0}^{n} q^{\binom{k+1}{2}}\binom{n+1}{k+1}_q z^{k+1} \;=\; \underbrace{\sum_{k=0}^{n} q^{\binom{k+1}{2}}\binom{n}{k+1}_q z^{k+1}}_{S_1} \;+\; \underbrace{\sum_{k=0}^{n} q^{\binom{k+1}{2}+n-k}\binom{n}{k}_q z^{k+1}}_{S_2}. \] \emph{Step C ($S_2 = z q^n\, Q_n(z)$).} The identity $\binom{k+1}{2} = \binom{k}{2} + k$ (helper \texttt{choose\_two\_succ}) and $k + (n - k) = n$ (valid because $k \leq n$, by \texttt{Nat.sub\_add\_cancel}) give $q^{\binom{k+1}{2}+n-k}\, z^{k+1} = z\, q^n \cdot q^{\binom{k}{2}}\, z^k$, hence \[ S_2 \;=\; z\, q^n \sum_{k=0}^{n} q^{\binom{k}{2}}\binom{n}{k}_q z^k \;=\; z\, q^n\, Q_n(z). \] \emph{Step D ($1 + S_1 = Q_n(z)$).} Reindex $j = k+1$ to identify $S_1 = \sum_{j=1}^{n+1} q^{\binom{j}{2}}\binom{n}{j}_q z^j$, then adjoin the $j = 0$ term $1$ (using \texttt{Finset.sum\_range\_succ'} in reverse): \[ 1 + S_1 \;=\; \sum_{j=0}^{n+1} q^{\binom{j}{2}}\binom{n}{j}_q z^j. \] The $j = n+1$ term vanishes by Lemma~\ref{lem:qBinom-eq-zero-of-lt} ($\binom{n}{n+1}_q = 0$), reducing this to $Q_n(z)$. Combining the four steps, $Q_{n+1}(z) = (1 + S_1) + S_2 = Q_n(z) + z q^n Q_n(z) = Q_n(z)\,(1 + z q^n)$. The final algebraic identity is closed in Lean by \texttt{linear\_combination}. \qedhere
nodes.statement_short: Induction on $n$. The inductive step splits $Q_{n+1}$ via q-Pascal into $1+S_1+S_2$ with $S_2=zq^nQ_n$ and $1+S_1=Q_n$.

nodes.name: Base case
nodes.statement: Induction on $n$, following the Lean proof \texttt{QSeries.prod\_one\_add\_mul\_pow\_eq\_sum\_qBinom} in \texttt{QSeries/FiniteBinomial.lean}. The case $n = 0$ gives $1 = 1$.

nodes.name: Reduce the inductive step
nodes.statement: For the inductive step, set $P_n(z) := \prod_{k=0}^{n-1}(1 + z q^k)$ and $Q_n(z) := \sum_{k=0}^{n} q^{\binom{k}{2}}\binom{n}{k}_q z^k$, so the theorem reads $P_n = Q_n$. By \texttt{Finset.prod\_range\_succ} and the inductive hypothesis $P_n = Q_n$, \[ P_{n+1}(z) \;=\; P_n(z)\,(1 + z q^n) \;=\; Q_n(z)\,(1 + z q^n), \] so it suffices to show $Q_{n+1}(z) = Q_n(z)\,(1 + z q^n)$. We decompose $Q_{n+1}(z) = \sum_{k=0}^{n+1} q^{\binom{k}{2}}\binom{n+1}{k}_q z^k$ in four explicit steps (mirroring \texttt{stepB}--\texttt{stepD} of the Lean proof).

nodes.name: Step A: peel off k=0
nodes.statement: \emph{Step A (peel off $k = 0$ via \texttt{Finset.sum\_range\_succ'}).} Using $\binom{n+1}{0}_q = 1$, \[ Q_{n+1}(z) \;=\; 1 \;+\; \sum_{k=0}^{n} q^{\binom{k+1}{2}}\,\binom{n+1}{k+1}_q\,z^{k+1}. \]

nodes.name: Step B: q-Pascal split
nodes.statement: \emph{Step B ($q$-Pascal split).} Apply Lemma~\ref{lem:qpascal} inside the sum and split via \texttt{Finset.sum\_add\_distrib}: \[ \sum_{k=0}^{n} q^{\binom{k+1}{2}}\binom{n+1}{k+1}_q z^{k+1} \;=\; \underbrace{\sum_{k=0}^{n} q^{\binom{k+1}{2}}\binom{n}{k+1}_q z^{k+1}}_{S_1} \;+\; \underbrace{\sum_{k=0}^{n} q^{\binom{k+1}{2}+n-k}\binom{n}{k}_q z^{k+1}}_{S_2}. \]
nodes.statement_short: Apply q-Pascal inside the sum, splitting into $S_1+S_2$.

nodes.name: Step C: S_2 = z q^n Q_n
nodes.statement: \emph{Step C ($S_2 = z q^n\, Q_n(z)$).} The identity $\binom{k+1}{2} = \binom{k}{2} + k$ (helper \texttt{choose\_two\_succ}) and $k + (n - k) = n$ (valid because $k \leq n$, by \texttt{Nat.sub\_add\_cancel}) give $q^{\binom{k+1}{2}+n-k}\, z^{k+1} = z\, q^n \cdot q^{\binom{k}{2}}\, z^k$, hence \[ S_2 \;=\; z\, q^n \sum_{k=0}^{n} q^{\binom{k}{2}}\binom{n}{k}_q z^k \;=\; z\, q^n\, Q_n(z). \]

nodes.name: Step D: 1 + S_1 = Q_n
nodes.statement: \emph{Step D ($1 + S_1 = Q_n(z)$).} Reindex $j = k+1$ to identify $S_1 = \sum_{j=1}^{n+1} q^{\binom{j}{2}}\binom{n}{j}_q z^j$, then adjoin the $j = 0$ term $1$ (using \texttt{Finset.sum\_range\_succ'} in reverse): \[ 1 + S_1 \;=\; \sum_{j=0}^{n+1} q^{\binom{j}{2}}\binom{n}{j}_q z^j. \] The $j = n+1$ term vanishes by Lemma~\ref{lem:qBinom-eq-zero-of-lt} ($\binom{n}{n+1}_q = 0$), reducing this to $Q_n(z)$.
nodes.statement_short: Reindex and use vanishing above the diagonal to get $1+S_1=Q_n(z)$.

nodes.name: Combine
nodes.statement: Combining the four steps, $Q_{n+1}(z) = (1 + S_1) + S_2 = Q_n(z) + z q^n Q_n(z) = Q_n(z)\,(1 + z q^n)$. The final algebraic identity is closed in Lean by \texttt{linear\_combination}. \qedhere

nodes.name: Proof of the Cauchy identity (Heine's argument)
nodes.statement: We follow Heine's classical functional-equation argument, which is the route realised in Lean (\texttt{QSeries.hasSum\_qPochhammer\_div\_mul\_pow}). Define \[ c_n \;:=\; \frac{(a;q)_n}{(q;q)_n}, \qquad F(z) \;:=\; \sum_{n \ge 0} c_n\, z^n, \qquad G(z) \;:=\; \frac{(a z;q)_\infty}{(z;q)_\infty}. \] The argument has three pieces. \emph{(i) Coefficient recurrence.} From $(a;q)_{n+1} = (a;q)_n(1 - a q^n)$ and $(q;q)_{n+1} = (q;q)_n(1 - q^{n+1})$, \[ c_{n+1}\,(1 - q^{n+1}) \;=\; c_n\,(1 - a q^n). \] (Note that $|q| < 1$ forces $1 - q^{n+1} \neq 0$, so $c_n$ is well-defined.) \emph{(ii) Functional equation $(1-z)\,H(z) = (1-az)\,H(qz)$ for $H \in \{F, G\}$.} For $F$: expand both sides as power series; the coefficient identity in (i) shows the series of $(1-z) F(z)$ and $(1-az) F(qz)$ agree term-by-term. The sum $F(z)$ converges absolutely on $\|z\| < 1$ because the coefficient sequence $c_n$ is bounded (its numerator $\|(a;q)_n\|$ converges by Lemma~\ref{lem:multipliable-one-sub-smul-qpow} and its denominator $\|(q;q)_n\|$ is eventually bounded below by a positive constant). For $G$: from the telescoping identity $(z;q)_\infty = (1-z)\,(zq;q)_\infty$ (an instance of $\prod_{k\ge 0} f_k = f_0 \cdot \prod_{k\ge 1} f_k$) applied to both $(z;q)_\infty$ and $(az;q)_\infty$. \emph{(iii) Iteration and passage to the limit.} Iterating the functional equation $n$ times on the open unit disc gives \[ F(z) \cdot (z;q)_n \;=\; F(q^n z) \cdot (a z;q)_n \] for every $n \ge 0$. As $n \to \infty$: \begin{itemize} \item $(z;q)_n \to (z;q)_\infty$ and $(az;q)_n \to (az;q)_\infty$ by Lemma~\ref{lem:multipliable-one-sub-smul-qpow} (the partial products of a multipliable family converge to its \texttt{tprod}); \item $F(q^n z) \to F(0) = c_0 = 1$: this is Tannery's theorem (\texttt{tendsto\_tsum\_of\_dominated\_convergence}) applied summand-by-summand, with the dominating bound $\|c_k (q^n z)^k\| \le C\,\|z\|^k$ (summable in $k$, uniformly in $n$). \end{itemize} Therefore $F(z) \cdot (z;q)_\infty = (a z;q)_\infty$. Since $\|z\| < 1$ implies $(z;q)_\infty \neq 0$ (no factor $1 - z q^k$ can be zero, by the norm estimate; combined with multipliability this gives non-vanishing of the \texttt{tprod}), we may divide to conclude $F(z) = G(z)$. \qedhere
nodes.statement_short: Heine's functional-equation argument: $F$ and $G$ both satisfy $(1-z)H(z)=(1-az)H(qz)$. Iterating and letting $n\to\infty$ (Tannery) gives $F=G$.

nodes.name: Setup: define c_n, F, G
nodes.statement: We follow Heine's classical functional-equation argument, which is the route realised in Lean (\texttt{QSeries.hasSum\_qPochhammer\_div\_mul\_pow}). Define \[ c_n \;:=\; \frac{(a;q)_n}{(q;q)_n}, \qquad F(z) \;:=\; \sum_{n \ge 0} c_n\, z^n, \qquad G(z) \;:=\; \frac{(a z;q)_\infty}{(z;q)_\infty}. \] The argument has three pieces.

nodes.name: (i) Coefficient recurrence

nodes.name: (ii) Functional equation
nodes.statement: \emph{(ii) Functional equation $(1-z)\,H(z) = (1-az)\,H(qz)$ for $H \in \{F, G\}$.} For $F$: expand both sides as power series; the coefficient identity in (i) shows the series of $(1-z) F(z)$ and $(1-az) F(qz)$ agree term-by-term. The sum $F(z)$ converges absolutely on $\|z\| < 1$ because the coefficient sequence $c_n$ is bounded (its numerator $\|(a;q)_n\|$ converges by Lemma~\ref{lem:multipliable-one-sub-smul-qpow} and its denominator $\|(q;q)_n\|$ is eventually bounded below by a positive constant). For $G$: from the telescoping identity $(z;q)_\infty = (1-z)\,(zq;q)_\infty$ (an instance of $\prod_{k\ge 0} f_k = f_0 \cdot \prod_{k\ge 1} f_k$) applied to both $(z;q)_\infty$ and $(az;q)_\infty$.
nodes.statement_short: Both $F$ and $G$ satisfy the functional equation.

nodes.name: Functional equation for F
nodes.statement: For $F$: expand both sides as power series; the coefficient identity in (i) shows the series of $(1-z) F(z)$ and $(1-az) F(qz)$ agree term-by-term. The sum $F(z)$ converges absolutely on $\|z\| < 1$ because the coefficient sequence $c_n$ is bounded (its numerator $\|(a;q)_n\|$ converges by Lemma~\ref{lem:multipliable-one-sub-smul-qpow} and its denominator $\|(q;q)_n\|$ is eventually bounded below by a positive constant).
nodes.statement_short: For $F$: coefficient recurrence gives it termwise; $F$ converges on the disc.

nodes.name: Functional equation for G
nodes.statement: For $G$: from the telescoping identity $(z;q)_\infty = (1-z)\,(zq;q)_\infty$ (an instance of $\prod_{k\ge 0} f_k = f_0 \cdot \prod_{k\ge 1} f_k$) applied to both $(z;q)_\infty$ and $(az;q)_\infty$.

nodes.name: (iii) Iteration and passage to the limit
nodes.statement: \emph{(iii) Iteration and passage to the limit.} Iterating the functional equation $n$ times on the open unit disc gives \[ F(z) \cdot (z;q)_n \;=\; F(q^n z) \cdot (a z;q)_n \] for every $n \ge 0$. As $n \to \infty$: \begin{itemize} \item $(z;q)_n \to (z;q)_\infty$ and $(az;q)_n \to (az;q)_\infty$ by Lemma~\ref{lem:multipliable-one-sub-smul-qpow} (the partial products of a multipliable family converge to its \texttt{tprod}); \item $F(q^n z) \to F(0) = c_0 = 1$: this is Tannery's theorem (\texttt{tendsto\_tsum\_of\_dominated\_convergence}) applied summand-by-summand, with the dominating bound $\|c_k (q^n z)^k\| \le C\,\|z\|^k$ (summable in $k$, uniformly in $n$). \end{itemize} Therefore $F(z) \cdot (z;q)_\infty = (a z;q)_\infty$. Since $\|z\| < 1$ implies $(z;q)_\infty \neq 0$ (no factor $1 - z q^k$ can be zero, by the norm estimate; combined with multipliability this gives non-vanishing of the \texttt{tprod}), we may divide to conclude $F(z) = G(z)$. \qedhere
nodes.statement_short: Iterate and pass to the limit to get $F=G$.

nodes.name: Iterate functional equation
nodes.statement: Iterating the functional equation $n$ times on the open unit disc gives \[ F(z) \cdot (z;q)_n \;=\; F(q^n z) \cdot (a z;q)_n \] for every $n \ge 0$. As $n \to \infty$: \begin{itemize}

nodes.name: Partial products converge
nodes.statement: $(z;q)_n \to (z;q)_\infty$ and $(az;q)_n \to (az;q)_\infty$ by Lemma~\ref{lem:multipliable-one-sub-smul-qpow} (the partial products of a multipliable family converge to its \texttt{tprod});

nodes.name: Tannery limit
nodes.statement: $F(q^n z) \to F(0) = c_0 = 1$: this is Tannery's theorem (\texttt{tendsto\_tsum\_of\_dominated\_convergence}) applied summand-by-summand, with the dominating bound $\|c_k (q^n z)^k\| \le C\,\|z\|^k$ (summable in $k$, uniformly in $n$). \end{itemize}

nodes.name: Divide by nonzero product
nodes.statement: Therefore $F(z) \cdot (z;q)_\infty = (a z;q)_\infty$. Since $\|z\| < 1$ implies $(z;q)_\infty \neq 0$ (no factor $1 - z q^k$ can be zero, by the norm estimate; combined with multipliability this gives non-vanishing of the \texttt{tprod}), we may divide to conclude $F(z) = G(z)$. \qedhere

nodes.name: Alternative route via a finite Cauchy-type analog
nodes.statement: A different classical route passes $n \to \infty$ in a Cauchy-type \emph{finite} analog \[ \sum_{k=0}^n \binom{n}{k}_q \frac{(a;q)_k}{(q;q)_k} z^k \;\xrightarrow{n \to \infty}\; \sum_{k=0}^\infty \frac{(a;q)_k}{(q;q)_k} z^k, \] using $(q;q)_k / (q;q)_n \to 1/(q^{k+1};q)_\infty$ and dominated convergence. The Heine route used above avoids the bookkeeping of a separate finite identity and is the one matched by the Lean formalisation.
nodes.statement_short: Alternative classical proof of the Cauchy identity: pass $n\to\infty$ in a finite Cauchy-type analog with dominated convergence.

nodes.name: Avoiding the infinite q-binomial theorem
nodes.statement: For Jacobi's triple product via Zhu's semi-finite proof, you do not actually need Theorem~\ref{thm:qbin-infinite}. You only need the \emph{first Euler identity} \[ (-z; q)_\infty = \sum_{n=0}^\infty \frac{q^{\binom{n}{2}}}{(q; q)_n} z^n, \] which is the $n \to \infty$ limit of Theorem~\ref{thm:qbin-finite} after rewriting $\prod_{k=0}^{n-1}(1 + zq^k)$ as $(-z; q)_n$ and dividing by suitable factors. This limit is gentler than the full Cauchy identity.
nodes.statement_short: For Zhu's proof of Jacobi's triple product only the Euler identity $(-z;q)_\infty=\sum q^{\binom n2}z^n/(q;q)_n$ is needed, a limit of the finite theorem.

nodes.name: Ambient commutative ring R
nodes.statement: Throughout this section $R$ is a commutative ring and $a, q \in R$.
nodes.section: 2 The $q$-Pochhammer symbol and Gaussian binomial coefficient (formalized)

nodes.name: Finite q-Pochhammer symbol
nodes.statement: For $n \in \mathbb{N}$, the finite $q$-Pochhammer symbol is \[ (a; q)_n \;:=\; \prod_{k = 0}^{n - 1} \bigl(1 - a\, q^k\bigr). \] In Lean, this is implemented as \texttt{$\prod$ k $\in$ Finset.range n, (1 - a * q\^{}k)}, specialising to $(a; q)_0 = 1$ (the empty product).
nodes.label: def:qPochhammer

nodes.name: Proof of base case
nodes.statement: The empty product is $1$ (\texttt{Finset.prod\_range\_zero}).

nodes.name: q-Pochhammer recurrence
nodes.statement: For all $n \in \mathbb{N}$, \[ (a; q)_{n+1} \;=\; (a; q)_n \cdot \bigl(1 - a\, q^n\bigr). \]
nodes.label: lem:qPochhammer-succ

nodes.name: Proof of recurrence
nodes.statement: Immediate from \texttt{Finset.prod\_range\_succ}.
nodes.statement_short: Immediate from splitting off the last factor of the product.

nodes.name: Gaussian binomial coefficient (recursive)
nodes.statement: The Gaussian binomial coefficient $\binom{n}{k}_q \in R$ is defined by recursion on $n$ and $k$: \[ \begin{aligned} \binom{0}{0}_q &= 1, & \binom{0}{k+1}_q &= 0, \\ \binom{n+1}{0}_q &= 1, & \binom{n+1}{k+1}_q &= \binom{n}{k+1}_q + q^{n-k}\,\binom{n}{k}_q. \end{aligned} \] This is the $q$-Pascal recurrence in the form stated in Lemma~\ref{lem:qpascal} (with the index shift $k \mapsto k+1$). By construction $\binom{n}{k}_q$ is a polynomial in $q$ with integer coefficients, defined for every pair $(n, k) \in \mathbb{N}^2$ (no division, no roots-of-unity exclusion).
nodes.statement_short: $\binom{n}{k}_q\in R$ defined by the q-Pascal recursion in $n,k$; a polynomial in $q$ with integer coefficients.
nodes.label: def:qBinom

nodes.name: Vanishing above the diagonal
nodes.statement: If $n < k$, then $\binom{n}{k}_q = 0$.
nodes.label: lem:qBinom-eq-zero-of-lt

nodes.name: Proof of vanishing above the diagonal
nodes.statement: Induction on $n$ and $k$ following the four-case recursive definition. The non-trivial case is $(n+1, k+1)$ with $n < k$: the recurrence gives $\binom{n+1}{k+1}_q = \binom{n}{k+1}_q + q^{n-k}\binom{n}{k}_q$, and both inductive hypotheses (at $(n, k+1)$ and $(n, k)$, available because $n < k + 1$ and $n < k$ respectively) yield $0$.
nodes.statement_short: Double induction on $n,k$ via the recursive definition; both inductive hypotheses give 0.

nodes.name: Diagonal value of Gaussian binomial
nodes.statement: $\binom{n}{n}_q = 1$ for every $n \in \mathbb{N}$.
nodes.label: lem:qBinom-self

nodes.name: Proof of diagonal value
nodes.statement: Induction on $n$. The case $n = 0$ is by definition. For the step, \[ \binom{n+1}{n+1}_q = \binom{n}{n+1}_q + q^{n-n}\,\binom{n}{n}_q = 0 + 1 \cdot 1 = 1, \] using Lemma~\ref{lem:qBinom-eq-zero-of-lt} for the first term and the inductive hypothesis for the second.
nodes.statement_short: Induction on $n$ using the recurrence and vanishing above the diagonal.

nodes.name: Base case
nodes.statement: Induction on $n$. The case $n = 0$ is by definition.

nodes.name: Inductive step
nodes.statement: For the step, \[ \binom{n+1}{n+1}_q = \binom{n}{n+1}_q + q^{n-n}\,\binom{n}{n}_q = 0 + 1 \cdot 1 = 1, \] using Lemma~\ref{lem:qBinom-eq-zero-of-lt} for the first term and the inductive hypothesis for the second.
nodes.statement_short: Recurrence plus vanishing lemma and hypothesis give 1.

nodes.name: Closed form for Gaussian binomial
nodes.statement: For all $k \leq n$, \[ \binom{n}{k}_q \cdot (q; q)_k \cdot (q; q)_{n - k} \;=\; (q; q)_n. \]
nodes.label: lem:qBinom-closed-form

nodes.name: Proof of closed form
nodes.statement: Induction on $n$. \emph{Base case $n = 0$.} Forces $k = 0$ and the identity is $1 \cdot 1 \cdot 1 = 1$. \emph{Boundary $k = 0$.} Reduces to $1 \cdot 1 \cdot (q; q)_n = (q; q)_n$. \emph{Boundary $k = n + 1$.} By Lemma~\ref{lem:qBinom-self} we have $\binom{n+1}{n+1}_q = 1$, and $(q; q)_0 = 1$, so both sides equal $(q; q)_{n+1}$. \emph{Inductive step $k + 1 \leq n$.} Apply the $q$-Pascal recurrence \[ \binom{n+1}{k+1}_q = \binom{n}{k+1}_q + q^{n-k}\,\binom{n}{k}_q \] and the factorisations \[ (q; q)_{n - k} \;=\; (q; q)_{n - (k+1)} \cdot \bigl(1 - q\,q^{n-(k+1)}\bigr), \qquad (q; q)_{k + 1} \;=\; (q; q)_k \cdot \bigl(1 - q\,q^k\bigr), \] together with the power identities $q \cdot q^{n-(k+1)} = q^{n-k}$ and $q^{n-k} \cdot (q \cdot q^k) = q \cdot q^n$, which use $k \leq n$ via \texttt{Nat.sub\_add\_cancel}. The two inductive hypotheses at $(n, k+1)$ and $(n, k)$ then combine into the required identity, dispatched in Lean by \texttt{linear\_combination}.
nodes.statement_short: Induction on $n$ with boundary cases $k=0$, $k=n+1$ and the inductive case via q-Pascal and factorisations.

nodes.name: Induction setup
nodes.statement: Induction on $n$.

nodes.name: Base case n=0
nodes.statement: \emph{Base case $n = 0$.} Forces $k = 0$ and the identity is $1 \cdot 1 \cdot 1 = 1$.

nodes.name: Boundary k=0
nodes.statement: \emph{Boundary $k = 0$.} Reduces to $1 \cdot 1 \cdot (q; q)_n = (q; q)_n$.

nodes.name: Boundary k=n+1
nodes.statement: \emph{Boundary $k = n + 1$.} By Lemma~\ref{lem:qBinom-self} we have $\binom{n+1}{n+1}_q = 1$, and $(q; q)_0 = 1$, so both sides equal $(q; q)_{n+1}$.

nodes.name: Inductive step
nodes.statement: \emph{Inductive step $k + 1 \leq n$.} Apply the $q$-Pascal recurrence \[ \binom{n+1}{k+1}_q = \binom{n}{k+1}_q + q^{n-k}\,\binom{n}{k}_q \] and the factorisations \[ (q; q)_{n - k} \;=\; (q; q)_{n - (k+1)} \cdot \bigl(1 - q\,q^{n-(k+1)}\bigr), \qquad (q; q)_{k + 1} \;=\; (q; q)_k \cdot \bigl(1 - q\,q^k\bigr), \] together with the power identities $q \cdot q^{n-(k+1)} = q^{n-k}$ and $q^{n-k} \cdot (q \cdot q^k) = q \cdot q^n$, which use $k \leq n$ via \texttt{Nat.sub\_add\_cancel}. The two inductive hypotheses at $(n, k+1)$ and $(n, k)$ then combine into the required identity, dispatched in Lean by \texttt{linear\_combination}.
nodes.statement_short: q-Pascal plus factorisations combine the two hypotheses.

nodes.name: Infinite q-Pochhammer symbol
nodes.statement: \[ (a; q)_\infty \;:=\; \prod_{k=0}^{\infty}\bigl(1 - a\, q^k\bigr) \;\in\; \mathbb{C}, \] defined unconditionally via \texttt{tprod}. The value is mathematically meaningful (and the product is convergent) under the hypothesis $\|q\| < 1$ provided by Lemma~\ref{lem:multipliable-one-sub-smul-qpow}.
nodes.section: 2.4 The infinite $q$-Pochhammer symbol and Cauchy identity (steps 6, 8)
nodes.label: def:qPochhammerInf

nodes.name: Multipliability of q-Pochhammer factors
nodes.statement: For $a, q \in \mathbb{C}$ with $\|q\| < 1$, the family $k \mapsto 1 - a\, q^k$ is multipliable; in particular the partial products converge to $(a; q)_\infty$.
nodes.section: 2.4 The infinite $q$-Pochhammer symbol and Cauchy identity (steps 6, 8)
conclusions: the family $k \mapsto 1 - a\, q^k$ is multipliable
in particular the partial products converge to $(a; q)_\infty$.
nodes.label: lem:multipliable-one-sub-smul-qpow

nodes.name: Proof of multipliability
nodes.statement: Reduce multipliability to summability of $\sum_k \|a q^k\|$ via Mathlib's \texttt{multipliable\_one\_add\_of\_summable} (which works in any complete normed ring), then bound $\|a q^k\| = \|a\|\, \|q\|^k$ and conclude by the geometric series $\sum_k \|q\|^k < \infty$ (\texttt{summable\_geometric\_of\_lt\_one}).
nodes.section: 2.4 The infinite $q$-Pochhammer symbol and Cauchy identity (steps 6, 8)
nodes.statement_short: Reduce to summability of $\sum\|aq^k\|$ and compare with a geometric series.

nodes.name: First Euler identity
nodes.statement: For $\|q\| < 1$ and $\|z\| < 1$, \[ \sum_{n=0}^{\infty} \frac{z^n}{(q;q)_n} = \frac{1}{(z;q)_\infty}. \]
nodes.label: lem:euler-first

nodes.name: Proof of first Euler identity
nodes.statement: Specialise the Cauchy identity (Theorem~\ref{thm:qbin-infinite-formalized}) at $a = 0$, using $(0;q)_n = 1$ and $(0\cdot z;q)_\infty = 1$.

nodes.name: Second Euler identity
nodes.statement: For $\|q\| < 1$ and $\|z\| < 1$, \[ \sum_{n=0}^{\infty} \frac{q^{\binom{n}{2}} z^n}{(q;q)_n} = (-z;q)_\infty. \]
nodes.label: lem:euler-second

nodes.name: Proof of second Euler identity
nodes.statement: Take $N \to \infty$ in the finite $q$-binomial theorem (Theorem~\ref{thm:qbin-finite}), rewriting $\prod_{k=0}^{N-1}(1 + z q^k) \to (-z;q)_\infty$ by Lemma~\ref{lem:multipliable-one-sub-smul-qpow} and replacing $\binom{N}{k}_q$ by $(q;q)_N / \bigl((q;q)_k (q;q)_{N-k}\bigr)$ (Lemma~\ref{lem:qBinom-closed-form}). The exchange of limit and sum is \texttt{tendsto\_tsum\_of\_dominated\_convergence}, with the dominating bound coming from $(q;q)_N / (q;q)_{N-k} \to 1$ being bounded uniformly in $N$. Summability of the target series is \texttt{QSeries.summable\_euler\_second}.
nodes.statement_short: Let $N\to\infty$ in the finite q-binomial theorem using the closed form and dominated convergence.

nodes.name: Pass to the limit
nodes.statement: Take $N \to \infty$ in the finite $q$-binomial theorem (Theorem~\ref{thm:qbin-finite}), rewriting $\prod_{k=0}^{N-1}(1 + z q^k) \to (-z;q)_\infty$ by Lemma~\ref{lem:multipliable-one-sub-smul-qpow} and replacing $\binom{N}{k}_q$ by $(q;q)_N / \bigl((q;q)_k (q;q)_{N-k}\bigr)$ (Lemma~\ref{lem:qBinom-closed-form}).
nodes.statement_short: Take $N\to\infty$ in the finite theorem, rewriting with multipliability and closed form.

nodes.name: Dominated convergence
nodes.statement: The exchange of limit and sum is \texttt{tendsto\_tsum\_of\_dominated\_convergence}, with the dominating bound coming from $(q;q)_N / (q;q)_{N-k} \to 1$ being bounded uniformly in $N$.
nodes.statement_short: Exchange limit and sum by dominated convergence.

nodes.name: Summability
nodes.statement: Summability of the target series is \texttt{QSeries.summable\_euler\_second}.

nodes.name: Telescoping of infinite q-Pochhammer
nodes.statement: For $\|q\| < 1$ and every $n$, \[ (q;q)_\infty \;=\; (q;q)_n \cdot (q^{\,n+1};q)_\infty. \]
nodes.section: 3.2 Expanding the product as a single series
nodes.label: lem:qPochhammerInf-telescope

nodes.name: Proof of telescoping
nodes.statement: Induction on $n$, using $(q;q)_{n+1} = (q;q)_n(1 - q^{n+1})$ (Lemma~\ref{lem:qPochhammer-succ}) and the recursion $(z;q)_\infty = (1-z)(zq;q)_\infty$ (\texttt{QSeries.qPochhammerInf\_eq\_one\_sub\_mul}).
nodes.section: 3.2 Expanding the product as a single series
nodes.statement_short: Induction on $n$ using the finite recurrence and the infinite-product recursion.

nodes.name: Product as a series
nodes.statement: For $\|q\| < 1$ and $\|z\| < 1$, \[ \sum_{n=0}^{\infty} q^{\binom{n}{2}} z^n\,(q^{\,n+1};q)_\infty = (q;q)_\infty\,(-z;q)_\infty. \]
nodes.section: 3.2 Expanding the product as a single series
nodes.label: lem:qPochhammerInf-prod-hassum

nodes.name: Proof of product as a series
nodes.statement: Multiply the second Euler identity (Lemma~\ref{lem:euler-second}) by the constant $(q;q)_\infty$ and rewrite $(q;q)_\infty/(q;q)_n = (q^{n+1};q)_\infty$ via Lemma~\ref{lem:qPochhammerInf-telescope}.
nodes.section: 3.2 Expanding the product as a single series
nodes.statement_short: Multiply the second Euler identity by $(q;q)_\infty$ and telescope.

nodes.name: Durfee rectangle identity
nodes.statement: This is the core of the formalisation, replacing both the coefficient-recurrence bookkeeping of Proof~1 and the complex analysis of Proof~3. After the Cauchy product is rearranged by diagonals, each diagonal coefficient is exactly one of the sums \[ S_k(q) \;:=\; \sum_{m=0}^{\infty} \frac{q^{\,m(m+k)}}{(q;q)_m\,(q;q)_{m+k}}, \] and all of them collapse to $1/(q;q)_\infty$. This is the classical \emph{Durfee rectangle identity}: combinatorially, $m\times(m+k)$ is the Durfee rectangle of a partition, contributing $q^{m(m+k)}$, with the regions to its right and below contributing $1/(q;q)_m$ and $1/(q;q)_{m+k}$; the $k=0$ case is the classical Durfee square identity. (See Andrews, \emph{The Theory of Partitions}, 1976, and Gessel, \emph{Some generalized Durfee square identities}, Discrete Math.\ \textbf{50} (1984).) What is specific to this formalisation is the proof: rather than the Young-diagram bijection, the identity is established \emph{analytically} through the contraction recurrence below, which is convenient to formalise in Lean.
nodes.statement_short: The diagonal sums $S_k$ all equal $1/(q;q)_\infty$, the classical Durfee rectangle identity, here proved analytically.

nodes.name: Key sum S_k
nodes.statement: For $\|q\| < 1$ and $k \in \mathbb{N}$, $S_k(q) := \sum_{m \ge 0} q^{m(m+k)} / \bigl((q;q)_m\,(q;q)_{m+k}\bigr)$.
nodes.label: def:S-sum

nodes.name: Summability of S_k
nodes.statement: For $\|q\| < 1$, the summand of $S_k$ is summable.
nodes.label: lem:summable-S

nodes.name: Proof of summability of S_k
nodes.statement: The denominators $(q;q)_m(q;q)_{m+k}$ are bounded below in norm by a positive constant (the partial products of a convergent infinite product with nonzero limit), so the summand is dominated by $C\,\|q\|^{m^2}$, which is summable.
nodes.statement_short: Denominators bounded below; summand dominated by $C\|q\|^{m^2}$.

nodes.name: Limit of S_k
nodes.statement: For $\|q\| < 1$, $S_k(q) \to 1/(q;q)_\infty$ as $k \to \infty$.
nodes.label: lem:S-sum-tendsto

nodes.name: Proof of limit of S_k
nodes.statement: The $m = 0$ term is $1/(q;q)_k \to 1/(q;q)_\infty$ (\texttt{tendsto\_qPochhammer} and non-vanishing of $(q;q)_\infty$). The tail $m \ge 1$ tends to $0$ by dominated convergence: each term $q^{m(m+k)}/\bigl((q;q)_m(q;q)_{m+k}\bigr) \to 0$ as $k \to \infty$, dominated by $\|q\|^{m^2}/C$.
nodes.statement_short: The $m=0$ term tends to $1/(q;q)_\infty$; the tail vanishes by dominated convergence.

nodes.name: Proof of recurrence for S_k
nodes.statement: Combine the two series term-by-term, using $(q;q)_{m+k+1} = (q;q)_{m+k}(1 - q^{m+k+1})$ to write $S_k - S_{k+1}$ as a single series, then split the numerator $1 - q^m - q^{m+k+1}$ and reindex the $(1 - q^m)$ part by $m \mapsto m+1$. The two pieces reassemble into $q^{k+1}(S_{k+2} - S_{k+1})$.
nodes.statement_short: Combine series termwise, split the numerator and reindex.

nodes.name: Key identity (Durfee rectangle identity)
nodes.statement: For $\|q\| < 1$ and every $k$, $\;S_k(q) = 1/(q;q)_\infty$.
nodes.label: thm:S-sum-eq

nodes.name: Proof of key identity
nodes.statement: Write $D_k = S_k - S_{k+1}$. Iterating Lemma~\ref{lem:S-sum-recurrence} $n$ times gives $\|D_k\| \le \|q\|^{\,n(2k+n+1)/2}\,\|D_{k+n}\|$. Since $D_{k+n} \to 0$ (Lemma~\ref{lem:S-sum-tendsto}) and $\|q\|^{\,\cdots} \to 0$, we get $D_k = 0$ for all $k$. Hence $S_k = S_0$ is constant in $k$, and its common value equals $\lim_{k} S_k = 1/(q;q)_\infty$.
nodes.statement_short: Contraction argument: iterate the recurrence to bound $D_k=S_k-S_{k+1}$ by a vanishing quantity, so $S_k$ is constant and equals its limit.

nodes.name: Contraction bound
nodes.statement: Write $D_k = S_k - S_{k+1}$. Iterating Lemma~\ref{lem:S-sum-recurrence} $n$ times gives $\|D_k\| \le \|q\|^{\,n(2k+n+1)/2}\,\|D_{k+n}\|$.
nodes.statement_short: Set $D_k=S_k-S_{k+1}$ and iterate the recurrence to bound it.

nodes.name: Differences vanish
nodes.statement: Since $D_{k+n} \to 0$ (Lemma~\ref{lem:S-sum-tendsto}) and $\|q\|^{\,\cdots} \to 0$, we get $D_k = 0$ for all $k$.

nodes.name: Conclude
nodes.statement: Hence $S_k = S_0$ is constant in $k$, and its common value equals $\lim_{k} S_k = 1/(q;q)_\infty$.
nodes.statement_short: $S_k$ is constant, equal to its limit $1/(q;q)_\infty$.

nodes.name: Non-negative diagonal coefficient
nodes.statement: For $\|q\| < 1$ and $k \ge 0$, \[ \sum_{m=0}^{\infty} q^{\binom{m+k}{2}}\,(q^{\,m+k+1};q)_\infty \cdot \frac{q^{\binom{m}{2}}\, q^{m}}{(q;q)_m} = q^{\binom{k}{2}}. \]
nodes.statement_short: The $k$-th non-negative diagonal sum of the Cauchy product equals $q^{\binom k2}$.
nodes.label: lem:cauchy-coeff-nonneg

nodes.name: Proof of non-negative diagonal coefficient
nodes.statement: Rewrite $(q^{m+k+1};q)_\infty = (q;q)_\infty/(q;q)_{m+k}$ (Lemma~\ref{lem:qPochhammerInf-telescope}) and use the arithmetic identity $\binom{m+k}{2} + \binom{m}{2} + m = \binom{k}{2} + m(m+k)$ to reduce the sum to $q^{\binom{k}{2}}\,(q;q)_\infty \cdot S_k(q)$. Apply Theorem~\ref{thm:S-sum-eq}.
nodes.statement_short: Telescope and use an arithmetic identity to reduce to $q^{\binom k2}(q;q)_\infty S_k$, then apply the key identity.

nodes.name: Negative diagonal coefficient
nodes.statement_short: The $l$-th negative diagonal sum of the Cauchy product equals $q^{\binom{l+2}{2}}$.
nodes.label: lem:cauchy-coeff-neg

nodes.name: Proof of negative diagonal coefficient
nodes.statement: As in Lemma~\ref{lem:cauchy-coeff-nonneg}, using the companion arithmetic identity $\binom{n}{2} + \binom{n+l+1}{2} + (n+l+1) = \binom{l+2}{2} + n(n+l+1)$ and the key identity $S_{l+1} = 1/(q;q)_\infty$ (Theorem~\ref{thm:S-sum-eq}).
nodes.statement_short: As for the non-negative case, with a companion arithmetic identity and $S_{l+1}=1/(q;q)_\infty$.

nodes.name: Series recursion for second Euler series
nodes.statement: For $\|q\| < 1$, the series $S(z) := \sum_n q^{\binom{n}{2}} z^n / (q;q)_n$ satisfies $S(z) = (1+z)\,S(qz)$.
nodes.label: lem:euler-second-recursion

nodes.name: Proof of series recursion
nodes.statement: A term-by-term algebraic identity: the difference of the $z$- and $qz$-series equals $z\,S(qz)$, using $(q;q)_{n} = (q;q)_{n-1}(1 - q^{n})$. Summability for all $z$ is \texttt{QSeries.summable\_euler\_second'}, proved by the ratio test (the ratio $\|q\|^n\|z\|/\|1 - q^{n+1}\| \to 0$).
nodes.statement_short: Termwise algebraic identity; summability for all $z$ by the ratio test.

nodes.name: Extended second Euler identity
nodes.statement: For $\|q\| < 1$ and \emph{every} $z\in\mathbb{C}$, \[ \sum_{n=0}^{\infty} \frac{q^{\binom{n}{2}} z^n}{(q;q)_n} = (-z;q)_\infty. \]
nodes.label: thm:euler-second-all

nodes.name: Proof of extended second Euler identity
nodes.statement: Given any $z$, choose $N$ with $\|z q^N\| < 1$. Iterating Lemma~\ref{lem:euler-second-recursion} $N$ times gives $S(z) = \prod_{k=0}^{N-1}(1 + z q^k)\cdot S(z q^N)$, and $S(z q^N) = (-z q^N;q)_\infty$ by the (small-argument) second Euler identity (Lemma~\ref{lem:euler-second}). The product $\prod_{k=0}^{N-1}(1 + z q^k)\cdot(-zq^N;q)_\infty = (-z;q)_\infty$ by repeated use of \texttt{QSeries.qPochhammerInf\_eq\_one\_sub\_mul}.
nodes.statement_short: Iterate the series recursion $N$ times until $\|zq^N\|<1$, then apply the small-argument identity.

nodes.name: Choose N
nodes.statement: Given any $z$, choose $N$ with $\|z q^N\| < 1$.

nodes.name: Iterate recursion and apply small-argument identity
nodes.statement: Iterating Lemma~\ref{lem:euler-second-recursion} $N$ times gives $S(z) = \prod_{k=0}^{N-1}(1 + z q^k)\cdot S(z q^N)$, and $S(z q^N) = (-z q^N;q)_\infty$ by the (small-argument) second Euler identity (Lemma~\ref{lem:euler-second}).
nodes.statement_short: Iterate the recursion and apply the second Euler identity at $zq^N$.

nodes.name: Reassemble product
nodes.statement: The product $\prod_{k=0}^{N-1}(1 + z q^k)\cdot(-zq^N;q)_\infty = (-z;q)_\infty$ by repeated use of \texttt{QSeries.qPochhammerInf\_eq\_one\_sub\_mul}.

nodes.name: Extended Euler identity at q/z
nodes.statement: For $\|q\| < 1$ and $z \neq 0$ (no annulus condition), \[ \sum_{m=0}^{\infty} \frac{q^{\binom{m}{2}}\, q^{m}\, z^{-m}}{(q;q)_m} = (-q/z;q)_\infty. \]
nodes.label: lem:euler-second-qoz-all

nodes.name: Proof of extended Euler identity at q/z
nodes.statement: Apply Theorem~\ref{thm:euler-second-all} at the point $q/z$ (valid for all $q/z$, hence all $z \neq 0$).
nodes.statement_short: Apply the extended identity at the point $q/z$.

nodes.name: Triple product and bilateral series
nodes.statement: $\mathrm{jacobiProd}(q,z) := (q;q)_\infty\,(-z;q)_\infty\,(-q/z;q)_\infty$, and the bilateral series $\mathrm{jacobiBilateral}(q,z) := \sum_{k\ge0} z^k q^{\binom{k}{2}} + \sum_{m\ge0} z^{-(m+1)} q^{\binom{m+2}{2}}$ (the non-negative and negative halves of $\sum_{k\in\mathbb{Z}} z^k q^{k(k-1)/2}$).
nodes.section: 3.5 The triple product and bilateral series
nodes.statement_short: jacobiProd $=(q;q)_\infty(-z;q)_\infty(-q/z;q)_\infty$; jacobiBilateral = the two halves of $\sum_k z^kq^{k(k-1)/2}$.
nodes.label: def:jacobiProd

nodes.name: Jacobi triple product
nodes.statement: For $\|q\| < 1$, $\|z\| < 1$, $z \neq 0$, $\;\mathrm{jacobiProd}(q,z) = \mathrm{jacobiBilateral}(q,z)$; that is, \[ (q;q)_\infty\,(-z;q)_\infty\,(-q/z;q)_\infty = \sum_{k\ge0} z^k q^{\binom{k}{2}} + \sum_{m\ge0} z^{-(m+1)} q^{\binom{m+2}{2}}. \]
nodes.label: thm:jtp-full

nodes.name: Proof of Jacobi triple product (analytic)
nodes.statement: Expand $(q;q)_\infty(-z;q)_\infty$ as a series (Lemma~\ref{lem:qPochhammerInf-prod-hassum}) and $(-q/z;q)_\infty$ via the \emph{extended} second Euler identity (Lemma~\ref{lem:euler-second-qoz-all}), which holds for every $z \neq 0$ with no lower bound on $\|z\|$. Their Cauchy product over $\mathbb{N}\times\mathbb{N}$ is summable (\texttt{Summable.mul\_norm}), so by \texttt{Summable.tsum\_prod} the double sum may be reordered. Partition $\mathbb{N}\times\mathbb{N}$ into the diagonals $n \ge m$ (index $k = n - m \ge 0$) and $n < m$ (index $l = m - n - 1 \ge 0$). The $k$-diagonal sum is $z^k q^{\binom{k}{2}}$ by Lemma~\ref{lem:cauchy-coeff-nonneg}, and the $l$-diagonal sum is $z^{-(l+1)} q^{\binom{l+2}{2}}$ by Lemma~\ref{lem:cauchy-coeff-neg}. Since the extended identity carries no annulus hypothesis, the argument runs directly on the full punctured disc $0 < \|z\| < 1$, with no separate continuation step.
nodes.statement_short: Form the Cauchy product of two second-Euler expansions, reorder by diagonals, and evaluate each diagonal by the coefficient lemmas.

nodes.name: Expand both factors
nodes.statement: Expand $(q;q)_\infty(-z;q)_\infty$ as a series (Lemma~\ref{lem:qPochhammerInf-prod-hassum}) and $(-q/z;q)_\infty$ via the \emph{extended} second Euler identity (Lemma~\ref{lem:euler-second-qoz-all}), which holds for every $z \neq 0$ with no lower bound on $\|z\|$.

nodes.name: Reorder Cauchy product
nodes.statement: Their Cauchy product over $\mathbb{N}\times\mathbb{N}$ is summable (\texttt{Summable.mul\_norm}), so by \texttt{Summable.tsum\_prod} the double sum may be reordered.
nodes.statement_short: The Cauchy product is summable so may be reordered.

nodes.name: Evaluate diagonals
nodes.statement: Partition $\mathbb{N}\times\mathbb{N}$ into the diagonals $n \ge m$ (index $k = n - m \ge 0$) and $n < m$ (index $l = m - n - 1 \ge 0$). The $k$-diagonal sum is $z^k q^{\binom{k}{2}}$ by Lemma~\ref{lem:cauchy-coeff-nonneg}, and the $l$-diagonal sum is $z^{-(l+1)} q^{\binom{l+2}{2}}$ by Lemma~\ref{lem:cauchy-coeff-neg}.
nodes.statement_short: Split into diagonals and evaluate via the coefficient lemmas.

nodes.name: Whole punctured disc
nodes.statement: Since the extended identity carries no annulus hypothesis, the argument runs directly on the full punctured disc $0 < \|z\| < 1$, with no separate continuation step.
nodes.statement_short: No annulus restriction, so it holds on the punctured disc.

nodes.name: Divergence from the outline
nodes.statement: Compared with the Euler / $q$-binomial route: the formalisation uses a \emph{genuine Cauchy product} of two second-Euler expansions, not Zhu's semi-finite truncation; the diagonal coefficients are evaluated through the classical Durfee rectangle identity (Theorem~\ref{thm:S-sum-eq}), but via its analytic contraction-recurrence proof rather than the usual Young-diagram bijection; and the argument is carried out directly on the whole punctured disc by strengthening the Euler identity to all $z$ (Theorem~\ref{thm:euler-second-all}), so it needs neither an annulus restriction with a separate extension step, the Liouville-type complex analysis of Proof~3, nor the coefficient bookkeeping of Proof~1. (Using Durfee rectangles to reach the Jacobi triple product is itself known; see W.\ Chu, \emph{Durfee rectangles and the Jacobi triple product identity}, Acta Math.\ Sinica \textbf{9} (1993), 24--26.)
nodes.statement_short: The formal proof uses a genuine Cauchy product, an analytic proof of the Durfee identity, and an extended Euler identity instead of the textbook routes.

nodes.name: Generalized pentagonal number
nodes.statement: $\omega(k) := \bigl(k(3k-1)/2\bigr)$ for $k \in \mathbb{Z}$ (the product $k(3k-1)$ is always even), realised in Lean as a natural number.
nodes.label: def:pentagonal

nodes.name: Proof of pentagonal number theorem from JTP
nodes.statement: Apply the Jacobi triple product (Theorem~\ref{thm:jtp-full}) with $q \mapsto q^3$ and $z \mapsto -q$; the hypotheses reduce to $\|{-}q\| < 1$ and $-q \neq 0$, both immediate for $0 < \|q\| < 1$ (the case $q = 0$ is trivial). The left-hand side $(q^3;q^3)_\infty(q;q^3)_\infty(q^2;q^3)_\infty$ is regrouped into $(q;q)_\infty$ by splitting the product $\prod_{n\ge1}(1 - q^n)$ into the three residue classes $\{3k+1\},\{3k+2\},\{3k+3\}$ modulo $3$. Matching the right-hand exponents $k^2$ (with sign $(-1)^k$) against $\omega(\pm k)$ gives the pentagonal series.
nodes.statement_short: Specialise Jacobi's triple product at $q\mapsto q^3$, $z\mapsto -q$ and regroup residue classes mod 3.

nodes.name: Specialise JTP
nodes.statement: Apply the Jacobi triple product (Theorem~\ref{thm:jtp-full}) with $q \mapsto q^3$ and $z \mapsto -q$; the hypotheses reduce to $\|{-}q\| < 1$ and $-q \neq 0$, both immediate for $0 < \|q\| < 1$ (the case $q = 0$ is trivial).

nodes.name: Regroup product
nodes.statement: The left-hand side $(q^3;q^3)_\infty(q;q^3)_\infty(q^2;q^3)_\infty$ is regrouped into $(q;q)_\infty$ by splitting the product $\prod_{n\ge1}(1 - q^n)$ into the three residue classes $\{3k+1\},\{3k+2\},\{3k+3\}$ modulo $3$.
nodes.statement_short: Regroup the product by residues mod 3 into $(q;q)_\infty$.

nodes.name: Match exponents
nodes.statement: Matching the right-hand exponents $k^2$ (with sign $(-1)^k$) against $\omega(\pm k)$ gives the pentagonal series.

nodes.name: Summability of bilateral series for all z
nodes.statement: For $\|q\| < 1$ and \emph{every} $z \in \mathbb{C}$, the non-negative part $\sum_{k \ge 0} z^k\, q^{\binom{k}{2}}$ is summable.
conclusions: the non-negative part $\sum_{k \ge 0} z^k\, q^{\binom{k}{2}}$ is summable.
nodes.label: thm:summable-nonneg-all

nodes.name: Proof of summability for all z
nodes.statement: The ratio of consecutive terms is $|z|\,|q|^n \to 0$, so the ratio test gives summability; the Weierstrass $M$-test with $M_k = R^k \|q\|^{\binom{k}{2}}$ (summable by a further ratio test) gives uniform convergence on $|z| \le R$.
nodes.statement_short: Ratio test, and Weierstrass M-test for uniform convergence on discs.

nodes.name: Locally uniform convergence of the product side
nodes.statement: For $\|q\| < 1$, the partial products $\prod_{k < N}(1 - q^{2k})(1 + zq^{2k-1})(1 + q^{2k-1}/z)$ converge \emph{locally uniformly} on $\{z \neq 0\}$ to $\mathrm{jacobiProd}(q,z)$.
conclusions: the partial products $\prod_{k < N}(1 - q^{2k})(1 + zq^{2k-1})(1 + q^{2k-1}/z)$ converge \emph{locally uniformly} on $\{z \neq 0\}$ to $\mathrm{jacobiProd}(q,z)$.
nodes.label: thm:jacobi-prod-luc

nodes.name: Proof of locally uniform convergence (product)
nodes.statement: On $\overline{B}(z_0, \|z_0\|/2)$ for any $z_0 \neq 0$: the factor $\prod(1 + (-z)q^k)$ is handled by the uniform convergence of $\prod(1 + a_k)$ on compacta (Weierstrass $M$-test with $\sum \|a_k\| < \infty$), and the factor $\prod(1 + (-q/z)q^k)$ uses the bound $\|-q/z\| \le 2\|q\|/\|z_0\|$ on that ball. Products of uniformly convergent bounded sequences converge uniformly.
nodes.statement_short: On small balls around $z_0\ne0$ use uniform convergence of $\prod(1+a_k)$ via the M-test.

nodes.name: Locally uniform convergence of the series side
nodes.statement: For $\|q\| < 1$, the bilateral partial sums $\sum_{|k| < N} z^k\, q^{\binom{k}{2}}$ converge \emph{locally uniformly} on $\{z \neq 0\}$ to $\mathrm{jacobiBilateral}(q,z)$.
conclusions: the bilateral partial sums $\sum_{|k| < N} z^k\, q^{\binom{k}{2}}$ converge \emph{locally uniformly} on $\{z \neq 0\}$ to $\mathrm{jacobiBilateral}(q,z)$.
nodes.label: thm:jacobi-series-luc

nodes.name: Proof of locally uniform convergence (series)
nodes.statement: The non-negative half is locally uniformly convergent everywhere by Theorem~\ref{thm:summable-nonneg-all} and the $M$-test. The negative half $\sum_{m \ge 0} z^{-(m+1)} q^{\binom{m+2}{2}}$ is uniformly convergent on $\{\|z^{-1}\| \le R'\}$; near any $z_0 \neq 0$ the ball $B(z_0, \|z_0\|/2)$ satisfies $\|z^{-1}\| \le 2/\|z_0\|$.
nodes.statement_short: M-test for the non-negative half; the negative half converges uniformly where $\|z^{-1}\|$ is bounded.

nodes.name: Analytic Jacobi triple product
nodes.statement: For $\|q\| < 1$ and every $z \neq 0$, \[ (q;q)_\infty\,(-z;q)_\infty\,(-q/z;q)_\infty = \sum_{k \ge 0} z^k\, q^{\binom{k}{2}} + \sum_{m \ge 0} z^{-(m+1)}\, q^{\binom{m+2}{2}}. \]
nodes.label: thm:jtp-analytic

nodes.name: Proof of analytic Jacobi triple product
nodes.statement:
Both sides are locally uniformly convergent on $\{z 
eq 0\}$ (Theorems~ef{thm:jacobi-prod-luc} and~ef{thm:jacobi-series-luc}). Both satisfy the functional equation $H(qz) = H(z)/z$ for all $z 
eq 0$. For any fixed $z 
eq 0$, choose $N$ large enough so that $\|q^N z\| < 1$. Then Theorem~ef{thm:jtp-full} (valid at $q^N z$) together with the iterated functional equation for both sides yields equality at $z$.
nodes.statement_short: Both sides satisfy $H(qz)=H(z)/z$; shift $z$ into the unit disc and use the restricted triple product.

nodes.name: Local uniform convergence
nodes.statement: Both sides are locally uniformly convergent on $\{z \neq 0\}$ (Theorems~\ref{thm:jacobi-prod-luc} and~\ref{thm:jacobi-series-luc}).

nodes.name: Functional equation
nodes.statement: Both satisfy the functional equation $H(qz) = H(z)/z$ for all $z \neq 0$.

nodes.name: Shift into disc and conclude
nodes.statement: For any fixed $z \neq 0$, choose $N$ large enough so that $\|q^N z\| < 1$. Then Theorem~\ref{thm:jtp-full} (valid at $q^N z$) together with the iterated functional equation for both sides yields equality at $z$.
nodes.statement_short: Choose $N$ with $\|q^Nz\|<1$ and transport equality back.

nodes.name: Key idea of the FPS proof
nodes.statement: The variable $q$ becomes the formal power series indeterminate $X \in R[\![ X]\!]$, while $z$ lives in the coefficient ring $A = \texttt{LaurentPolynomial}\,\mathbb{C}$ (with $z = T(1)$, $z^{-1} = T(-1)$). The infinite $q$-Pochhammer symbol $(a; X)_\infty$ is a well-defined element of $R[\![ X]\!]$ because the factors $(1 - a X^k)$ converge to $1$ in the pi topology: each factor affects only finitely many coefficients of any fixed degree.
nodes.statement_short: In the FPS proof $q$ becomes the indeterminate $X$ and $z$ a Laurent-polynomial coefficient; $(a;X)_\infty$ converges $X$-adically.

nodes.name: Coefficient ring R for FPS section
nodes.statement: Throughout this section $R$ is a commutative ring (with \texttt{DiscreteTopology}).

nodes.name: FPS finite q-Pochhammer symbol
nodes.statement: For $a \in R[\![ X]\!]$ and $n \in \mathbb{N}$, \[ \texttt{qPoch}\,a\,n \;:=\; \prod_{k=0}^{n-1}\bigl(1 - a\cdot X^k\bigr) \;\in\; R[\![ X]\!]. \]
nodes.label: def:fps-qPoch

nodes.name: FPS base case
nodes.statement: $\texttt{qPoch}\,a\,0 = 1$.
nodes.label: lem:fps-qPoch-zero

nodes.name: Proof of FPS base case
nodes.statement: Empty product.

nodes.name: FPS recurrence
nodes.statement: $\texttt{qPoch}\,a\,(n+1) = \texttt{qPoch}\,a\,n \cdot (1 - a\cdot X^n)$.
nodes.label: lem:fps-qPoch-succ

nodes.name: Proof of FPS recurrence
nodes.statement: Immediate from \texttt{Finset.prod\_range\_succ}.

nodes.name: FPS shift identity
nodes.statement: $\texttt{qPoch}\,a\,(n+1) = (1-a)\cdot\texttt{qPoch}\,(aX)\,n$.
nodes.label: lem:fps-qPoch-shift

nodes.name: Proof of FPS shift identity
nodes.statement: Induction on $n$ using the recurrence.

nodes.name: Coefficient stabilisation
nodes.statement: If $d < n$ then $[X^d]\,\texttt{qPoch}\,a\,(n+1) = [X^d]\,\texttt{qPoch}\,a\,n$.
nodes.label: lem:fps-coeff-stable

nodes.name: Proof of coefficient stabilisation
nodes.statement: The new factor $(1 - a X^n)$ only affects monomials of degree $\ge n > d$.
nodes.statement_short: The new factor only affects degrees $\ge n$.

nodes.name: Constant coefficient of qPoch X n
nodes.statement: The constant term of $\texttt{qPoch}\,(X : R[\![ X]\!])\,n$ is $1$.
conclusions: The constant term of $\texttt{qPoch}\,(X : R[\![ X]\!])\,n$ is $1$.
nodes.label: lem:fps-constantCoeff-qPoch-X

nodes.name: Proof of constant coefficient
nodes.statement: Induction on $n$; each factor $(1 - X \cdot X^k)$ has constant term $1$.
nodes.statement_short: Induction; each factor has constant term 1.

nodes.name: FPS multipliability in pi topology
nodes.statement: The family $k \mapsto 1 - a\cdot X^k$ is multipliable in $R[\![ X]\!]$ (with the pi / $X$-adic topology).
conclusions: The family $k \mapsto 1 - a\cdot X^k$ is multipliable in $R[\![ X]\!]$
nodes.label: thm:fps-multipliable

nodes.name: Proof of FPS multipliability
nodes.statement: Apply \texttt{MvPowerSeries.WithPiTopology.multipliable\_one\_add\_of\_tendsto\_order\_atTop\_nhds\_top}: the $X$-adic order of $-(a X^k)$ is $\ge k$ (the factor $-(a X^k)$ is divisible by $X^k$), so the orders tend to $\infty$, which is the criterion for multipliability in the pi topology. No norm hypothesis is needed.
nodes.statement_short: $X$-adic orders of $-(aX^k)$ tend to infinity, the pi-topology multipliability criterion.

nodes.name: FPS infinite q-Pochhammer symbol
nodes.statement: \[ \texttt{qPochInf}\,a \;:=\; \prod_{k=0}^{\infty}\bigl(1 - a\cdot X^k\bigr) \;\in\; R[\![ X]\!]. \]
nodes.label: def:fps-qPochInf

nodes.name: FPS coefficient formula
nodes.statement: $[X^d]\,\texttt{qPochInf}\,a = [X^d]\,\texttt{qPoch}\,a\,(d+1)$.
nodes.label: lem:fps-coeff-qPochInf

nodes.name: Proof of FPS coefficient formula
nodes.statement: The partial products stabilise at degree $d$ once $n > d$ (Lemma~\ref{lem:fps-coeff-stable}), and converge to $\texttt{qPochInf}\,a$ in the pi topology; continuity of coefficient extraction gives the identity.
nodes.statement_short: Partial products stabilise in degree $d$ and converge; coefficient extraction is continuous.

nodes.name: FPS recursion
nodes.statement: $\texttt{qPochInf}\,a = (1-a)\cdot\texttt{qPochInf}\,(a\cdot X)$.
nodes.label: lem:fps-qPochInf-recursion

nodes.name: Proof of FPS recursion
nodes.statement: Extract the $k=0$ factor from the infinite product and shift: $\prod_{k\ge 0}(1-a X^k) = (1-a)\cdot\prod_{k\ge 0}(1 - a X^{k+1}) = (1-a)\cdot\texttt{qPochInf}(aX)$.
nodes.statement_short: Extract the $k=0$ factor and shift the index.

nodes.name: FPS iterated telescoping
nodes.statement: For every $n \in \mathbb{N}$: $\texttt{qPochInf}\,a = \texttt{qPoch}\,a\,n \cdot \texttt{qPochInf}\,(a\cdot X^n)$.
nodes.label: lem:fps-qPochInf-eq-qPoch-mul

nodes.name: Proof of FPS iterated telescoping
nodes.statement: Induction on $n$ using Lemma~\ref{lem:fps-qPochInf-recursion}.
nodes.statement_short: Induction on $n$ using the FPS recursion.

nodes.name: FPS unit
nodes.statement: If $1 - [X^0]\,a$ is a unit of $R$, then $\texttt{qPochInf}\,a$ is a unit of $R[\![ X]\!]$.
conclusions: then $\texttt{qPochInf}\,a$ is a unit of $R[\![ X]\!]$.
nodes.label: lem:fps-isUnit-qPochInf

nodes.name: Proof of FPS unit
nodes.statement: The constant term of $\texttt{qPochInf}\,a$ equals $1 - [X^0]\,a$ (which is a unit), and a power series with unit constant term is a unit.
nodes.statement_short: Constant term is a unit, so the power series is a unit.

nodes.name: FPS Euler second identity
nodes.statement: In $R[\![ X]\!]$ (for any commutative ring $R$ with discrete topology), \[ \texttt{qPochInf}(-a) \;=\; \sum_{k=0}^{\infty} X^{\binom{k}{2}}\cdot a^k \cdot \bigl(\texttt{qPoch}\,(X : R[\![ X]\!])\,k\bigr)^{-1}. \]
assumptions: In $R[\![ X]\!]$ (for any commutative ring $R$ with discrete topology),
nodes.label: thm:fps-euler-second

nodes.name: Proof of FPS Euler second identity
nodes.statement: At each degree $d$, only finitely many terms contribute (those with $\binom{k}{2} \le d$, i.e.\ $k \le d+1$). The key algebraic step is: $[X^j]\,\texttt{qBinom}(N, k, X) = [X^j]\,(\texttt{qPoch}(X,k))^{-1}$ whenever $j + k \le N$ (\texttt{coeff\_qBinom\_eq\_qPochInv}). Then the finite $q$-binomial theorem (Theorem~\ref{thm:qbin-finite} with $z = -a$) gives $\texttt{qPoch}(-a, N) = \sum_{k=0}^{N} X^{\binom{k}{2}} \texttt{qBinom}(N,k,X) (-a)^k$ in $R[\![ X]\!]$. Taking $N = d+1$ and extracting the degree-$d$ coefficient yields the identity at each degree. The sum is summable (each degree has finitely many nonzero contributions) and the tsum specialises to the tprod as $N \to \infty$ in the pi topology.
nodes.statement_short: Coefficientwise: compare degree-$d$ coefficients with the finite q-binomial theorem at $N=d+1$.

nodes.name: Finitely many contributions
nodes.statement: At each degree $d$, only finitely many terms contribute (those with $\binom{k}{2} \le d$, i.e.\ $k \le d+1$).
nodes.statement_short: Only finitely many terms contribute in each degree.

nodes.name: Coefficient identity
nodes.statement: The key algebraic step is: $[X^j]\,\texttt{qBinom}(N, k, X) = [X^j]\,(\texttt{qPoch}(X,k))^{-1}$ whenever $j + k \le N$ (\texttt{coeff\_qBinom\_eq\_qPochInv}).
nodes.statement_short: Coefficients of qBinom agree with those of $(\texttt{qPoch}(X,k))^{-1}$ in low degree.

nodes.name: Apply finite q-binomial
nodes.statement: Then the finite $q$-binomial theorem (Theorem~\ref{thm:qbin-finite} with $z = -a$) gives $\texttt{qPoch}(-a, N) = \sum_{k=0}^{N} X^{\binom{k}{2}} \texttt{qBinom}(N,k,X) (-a)^k$ in $R[\![ X]\!]$.

nodes.name: Extract degree d
nodes.statement: Taking $N = d+1$ and extracting the degree-$d$ coefficient yields the identity at each degree.

nodes.name: Summability and limit
nodes.statement: The sum is summable (each degree has finitely many nonzero contributions) and the tsum specialises to the tprod as $N \to \infty$ in the pi topology.
nodes.statement_short: Sum is summable and tsum agrees with tprod.

nodes.name: FPS key sum
nodes.statement: For $k \in \mathbb{N}$, define \[ S^{\mathrm{fps}}_k \;:=\; \sum_{m=0}^{\infty} X^{m(m+k)} \cdot \bigl(\texttt{qPoch}(X,m)\bigr)^{-1} \cdot \bigl(\texttt{qPoch}(X,m+k)\bigr)^{-1} \;\in\; R[\![ X]\!]. \]
nodes.label: def:fps-S

nodes.name: FPS key sum is summable
nodes.statement: The summand of $S^{\mathrm{fps}}_k$ is summable in $R[\![ X]\!]$.
conclusions: The summand of $S^{\mathrm{fps}}_k$ is summable in $R[\![ X]\!]$.
nodes.label: lem:fps-summable-S

nodes.name: Proof of FPS key sum summability
nodes.statement: The monomial $X^{m(m+k)}$ has $X$-adic order $\ge m$; since $m \to \infty$, the summand family satisfies the pi-topology criterion for summability.
nodes.statement_short: $X$-adic orders of summands tend to infinity.

nodes.name: FPS key sum recurrence
nodes.statement: For every $k$: \[ S^{\mathrm{fps}}_k - S^{\mathrm{fps}}_{k+1} \;=\; X^{k+1}\cdot\bigl(S^{\mathrm{fps}}_{k+2} - S^{\mathrm{fps}}_{k+1}\bigr). \]
nodes.label: lem:fps-S-recurrence

nodes.name: Proof of FPS key sum recurrence
nodes.statement: Combine the two series term-by-term. Write $(\texttt{qPoch}(X, m+k))^{-1} = (1 - X^{m+k+1})\cdot (\texttt{qPoch}(X, m+k+1))^{-1}$ (\texttt{qPochInv\_succ\_mul}), split the numerator, and reindex the $(1-X^m)$-part by $m \mapsto m+1$. This is a \emph{purely algebraic} ring identity in $R[\![ X]\!]$; no norms are needed.
nodes.statement_short: Termwise combination, numerator split and reindexing; a ring identity.

nodes.name: FPS: all S_k are equal
nodes.statement: $S^{\mathrm{fps}}_k = S^{\mathrm{fps}}_0$ for all $k \in \mathbb{N}$.
nodes.label: thm:fps-S-const

nodes.name: Proof that all FPS S_k are equal
nodes.statement: Let $D_k = S^{\mathrm{fps}}_k - S^{\mathrm{fps}}_{k+1}$. By Lemma~\ref{lem:fps-S-recurrence}, $D_k = X^{k+1} D_{k+2} + X^{k+1} D_{k+1}$; iterating, $[X^d]\,D_k = 0$ for all $d < k+1$ (directly from the recurrence, since $[X^d]\,X^{k+1} = 0$ when $d < k+1$). For $d \ge k+1$, induction on $d$ using the recurrence (strong induction) yields $[X^d]\,D_k = 0$ as well, because the only contributing term $[X^{k+1}]X^{k+1} = 1$ forces $[X^{d-(k+1)}]\,D_{k+2} = [X^{d-(k+1)}]\,D_k$ and the argument closes by strong induction. Hence $D_k = 0$ for all $k$, giving $S^{\mathrm{fps}}_k = S^{\mathrm{fps}}_0$.
nodes.statement_short: Show every coefficient of $D_k=S_k-S_{k+1}$ vanishes, by the recurrence and strong induction on degree.

nodes.name: Low-degree coefficients vanish
nodes.statement: Let $D_k = S^{\mathrm{fps}}_k - S^{\mathrm{fps}}_{k+1}$. By Lemma~\ref{lem:fps-S-recurrence}, $D_k = X^{k+1} D_{k+2} + X^{k+1} D_{k+1}$; iterating, $[X^d]\,D_k = 0$ for all $d < k+1$ (directly from the recurrence, since $[X^d]\,X^{k+1} = 0$ when $d < k+1$).
nodes.statement_short: Define $D_k$; recurrence kills coefficients below degree $k+1$.

nodes.name: Strong induction on degree
nodes.statement: For $d \ge k+1$, induction on $d$ using the recurrence (strong induction) yields $[X^d]\,D_k = 0$ as well, because the only contributing term $[X^{k+1}]X^{k+1} = 1$ forces $[X^{d-(k+1)}]\,D_{k+2} = [X^{d-(k+1)}]\,D_k$ and the argument closes by strong induction.
nodes.statement_short: Strong induction on $d$ for higher coefficients.

nodes.name: Conclude
nodes.statement: Hence $D_k = 0$ for all $k$, giving $S^{\mathrm{fps}}_k = S^{\mathrm{fps}}_0$.

nodes.name: FPS key identity
nodes.statement: For every $k$, \[ S^{\mathrm{fps}}_k \;=\; \bigl(\texttt{qPochInf}(X)\bigr)^{-1} \;=:\; \texttt{qqInv}. \]
nodes.label: thm:fps-key

nodes.name: Proof of FPS key identity
nodes.statement: By Theorem~\ref{thm:fps-S-const}, $S^{\mathrm{fps}}_k = S^{\mathrm{fps}}_{d+1}$ for any $d$. For $k = d+1 > d$, the only term contributing to $[X^d]\,S^{\mathrm{fps}}_{d+1}$ is $m=0$ (the $X^{0}$ monomial), giving $[X^d]\,(\texttt{qPoch}(X,d+1))^{-1}$. For $d+1$ steps of the recursion \texttt{qPochInf}$= $\texttt{qPoch}$(X,n)\cdot$\texttt{qPochInf}$(X \cdot X^n)$, one shows $[X^d]\,(\texttt{qPoch}(X,k))^{-1} = [X^d]\,\texttt{qqInv}$ for $d < k$ (Lemma \texttt{coeff\_qPochInv\_eq\_qqInv}). Hence $[X^d]\,S^{\mathrm{fps}}_k = [X^d]\,\texttt{qqInv}$ for all $d$.
nodes.statement_short: Coefficient by coefficient: replace $k$ by $d+1$, where only the $m=0$ term contributes, and compare with qqInv.

nodes.name: Shift index
nodes.statement: By Theorem~\ref{thm:fps-S-const}, $S^{\mathrm{fps}}_k = S^{\mathrm{fps}}_{d+1}$ for any $d$.

nodes.name: Only m=0 contributes
nodes.statement: For $k = d+1 > d$, the only term contributing to $[X^d]\,S^{\mathrm{fps}}_{d+1}$ is $m=0$ (the $X^{0}$ monomial), giving $[X^d]\,(\texttt{qPoch}(X,d+1))^{-1}$.
nodes.statement_short: Only the $m=0$ term contributes in degree $d$.

nodes.name: Compare with qqInv
nodes.statement: For $d+1$ steps of the recursion \texttt{qPochInf}$= $\texttt{qPoch}$(X,n)\cdot$\texttt{qPochInf}$(X \cdot X^n)$, one shows $[X^d]\,(\texttt{qPoch}(X,k))^{-1} = [X^d]\,\texttt{qqInv}$ for $d < k$ (Lemma \texttt{coeff\_qPochInv\_eq\_qqInv}).
nodes.statement_short: Low coefficients of $(\texttt{qPoch}(X,k))^{-1}$ agree with qqInv.

nodes.name: Conclude
nodes.statement: Hence $[X^d]\,S^{\mathrm{fps}}_k = [X^d]\,\texttt{qqInv}$ for all $d$.

nodes.name: Comparison with the analytic key identity
nodes.statement: The analytic key identity (Theorem~\ref{thm:S-sum-eq}) proves $S_k = 1/(q;q)_\infty$ using a \emph{norm estimate}: $\|D_k\| \le \|q\|^{n(2k+n+1)/2} \|D_{k+n}\| \to 0$. The FPS key identity (Theorem~\ref{thm:fps-key}) proves the same identity \emph{coefficient by coefficient} using only ring arithmetic in $R[\![ X ]\!]$, requiring no analytic hypotheses whatsoever.
nodes.statement_short: Analytic key identity uses a norm estimate; the FPS version works coefficientwise with ring arithmetic only.

nodes.name: FPS product expansion
nodes.statement: In $R[\![ X]\!]$: \[ \texttt{qPochInf}(X)\cdot\texttt{qPochInf}(-a) \;=\; \sum_{n=0}^{\infty} X^{\binom{n}{2}}\,a^n\, \texttt{qPochInf}(X \cdot X^n). \]
nodes.label: lem:fps-qqInf-euler2

nodes.name: Proof of FPS product expansion
nodes.statement: Expand $\texttt{qPochInf}(-a)$ via Theorem~\ref{thm:fps-euler-second} and distribute $\texttt{qPochInf}(X)$ through the tsum. The identity $\texttt{qPochInf}(X)\cdot(\texttt{qPoch}(X,n))^{-1} = \texttt{qPochInf}(X\cdot X^n)$ (Lemma~\ref{lem:fps-qPochInf-eq-qPoch-mul}) converts each term.
nodes.statement_short: Expand via the FPS Euler identity and telescope each term.

nodes.name: FPS Cauchy coefficient, non-negative diagonal
nodes.statement: For every $k \ge 0$: \[ \sum_{m=0}^{\infty} \bigl[X^{(m+k)\text{.choose}\,2}\cdot\texttt{qPochInf}(X\cdot X^{m+k})\bigr] \cdot \bigl[X^{m\text{.choose}\,2}\cdot X^m \cdot (\texttt{qPoch}(X,m))^{-1}\bigr] \;=\; X^{k\text{.choose}\,2}. \] That is, the $k$-th diagonal sum of the Cauchy product equals $X^{\binom{k}{2}}$.
conclusions: That is, the $k$-th diagonal sum of the Cauchy product equals $X^{\binom{k}{2}}$.
nodes.label: thm:fps-cauchy-nonneg

nodes.name: Proof of FPS non-negative diagonal
nodes.statement: The diagonal sum equals $X^{\binom{k}{2}}\cdot\texttt{qPochInf}(X)\cdot S^{\mathrm{fps}}_k$ after applying the arithmetic identity $\binom{m+k}{2} + \binom{m}{2} + m = \binom{k}{2} + m(m+k)$ (\texttt{choose2\_add}) and Lemma~\ref{lem:fps-qPochInf-eq-qPoch-mul}. Apply Theorem~\ref{thm:fps-key} and $\texttt{qPochInf}(X)\cdot\texttt{qqInv} = 1$.
nodes.statement_short: Reduce to $X^{\binom k2}\,\texttt{qPochInf}(X) S^{fps}_k$ and apply the FPS key identity.

nodes.name: FPS Cauchy coefficient, negative diagonal
nodes.statement: For every $l \ge 0$: \[ \sum_{n=0}^{\infty} \bigl[X^{n\text{.choose}\,2}\cdot\texttt{qPochInf}(X\cdot X^n)\bigr] \cdot \bigl[X^{(n+l+1)\text{.choose}\,2}\cdot X^{n+l+1} \cdot (\texttt{qPoch}(X,n+l+1))^{-1}\bigr] \;=\; X^{(l+2)\text{.choose}\,2}. \]
nodes.label: thm:fps-cauchy-neg

nodes.name: Proof of FPS negative diagonal
nodes.statement: Analogous to Theorem~\ref{thm:fps-cauchy-nonneg}, using the companion arithmetic identity $\binom{n}{2} + \binom{n+l+1}{2} + (n+l+1) = \binom{l+2}{2} + n(n+l+1)$ (\texttt{choose2\_add'}) and $S^{\mathrm{fps}}_{l+1} = \texttt{qqInv}$.
nodes.statement_short: Analogous, with the companion arithmetic identity and $S^{fps}_{l+1}=\texttt{qqInv}$.

nodes.name: FPS JTP objects
nodes.statement: Let $A = \texttt{LaurentPolynomial}\,\mathbb{C}$, $z = T(1)$, $z^{-1} = T(-1)$ viewed as constant power series in $A[\![ X]\!]$. Define: \begin{align*} \texttt{jtpProd} &\;:=\; \texttt{qPochInf}(X)\cdot\texttt{qPochInf}(-z)\cdot\texttt{qPochInf}(-X\cdot z^{-1}) \;\in\; A[\![ X]\!], \\ \texttt{jtpSeries} &\;:=\; \Bigl(\sum_{n\ge 0} T(n)\cdot X^{n\text{.choose}\,2}\Bigr) + \Bigl(\sum_{m\ge 0} T(-(m+1))\cdot X^{(m+2)\text{.choose}\,2}\Bigr) \;\in\; A[\![ X]\!]. \end{align*} Here $T(k)$ is the degree-$k$ monomial in the Laurent polynomial ring $A$, so $T(n) = z^n$ and $T(-(m+1)) = z^{-(m+1)}$.
nodes.statement_short: Over $A=$ Laurent polynomials, jtpProd is the triple product and jtpSeries the bilateral series in $A[[X]]$.
nodes.label: def:fps-jtp

nodes.name: FPS Jacobi triple product
nodes.statement: In $A[\![ X]\!]$ (with $A = \texttt{LaurentPolynomial}\,\mathbb{C}$): \[ \texttt{jtpProd} \;=\; \texttt{jtpSeries}, \] that is, \[ \texttt{qPochInf}(X)\cdot\texttt{qPochInf}(-z)\cdot\texttt{qPochInf}(-X/z) \;=\; \sum_{k \ge 0} z^k X^{\binom{k}{2}} \;+\; \sum_{m \ge 0} z^{-(m+1)} X^{\binom{m+2}{2}}. \]
nodes.label: thm:fps-jtp

nodes.name: Proof of FPS Jacobi triple product
nodes.statement: Expand \texttt{jtpProd} using Lemma~\ref{lem:fps-qqInf-euler2} (on the $\texttt{qPochInf}(X)\cdot\texttt{qPochInf}(-z)$ factor) and Theorem~\ref{thm:fps-euler-second} (on $\texttt{qPochInf}(-X z^{-1})$), forming a double tsum over $\mathbb{N}\times\mathbb{N}$. Summability of the double product $a_n \cdot b_m$ (where $a_n = X^{\binom{n}{2}} z^n \texttt{qPochInf}(X\cdot X^n)$ and $b_m = X^{\binom{m}{2}+m} z^{-m} (\texttt{qPoch}(X,m))^{-1}$) follows from the pi-topology structure: each coefficient of $a_n \cdot b_m$ is eventually zero in $n$ (once $\binom{n}{2} > d$) and in $m$ (once $\binom{m}{2}+m > d$). Partition $\mathbb{N}\times\mathbb{N}$ via the bijection $\mathtt{diagEquiv} : (n,m) \mapsto \text{inl}(n-m,m)$ if $m \le n$, $\text{inr}(m-n-1,n)$ otherwise. The $k$-diagonal $(m \le n, k = n-m)$ sum equals $z^k X^{\binom{k}{2}}$ by Theorem~\ref{thm:fps-cauchy-nonneg}; the $l$-diagonal $(m > n, l = m-n-1)$ sum equals $z^{-(l+1)} X^{\binom{l+2}{2}}$ by Theorem~\ref{thm:fps-cauchy-neg}. Summing over all $k$ and $l$ gives \texttt{jtpSeries}.
nodes.statement_short: Cauchy product of the two FPS Euler expansions, split by a diagonal bijection, with each diagonal evaluated by the coefficient theorems.

nodes.name: Expand
nodes.statement: Expand \texttt{jtpProd} using Lemma~\ref{lem:fps-qqInf-euler2} (on the $\texttt{qPochInf}(X)\cdot\texttt{qPochInf}(-z)$ factor) and Theorem~\ref{thm:fps-euler-second} (on $\texttt{qPochInf}(-X z^{-1})$), forming a double tsum over $\mathbb{N}\times\mathbb{N}$.
nodes.statement_short: Expand both factors into a double tsum.

nodes.name: Summability
nodes.statement: Summability of the double product $a_n \cdot b_m$ (where $a_n = X^{\binom{n}{2}} z^n \texttt{qPochInf}(X\cdot X^n)$ and $b_m = X^{\binom{m}{2}+m} z^{-m} (\texttt{qPoch}(X,m))^{-1}$) follows from the pi-topology structure: each coefficient of $a_n \cdot b_m$ is eventually zero in $n$ (once $\binom{n}{2} > d$) and in $m$ (once $\binom{m}{2}+m > d$).
nodes.statement_short: Double family is summable in the pi topology.

nodes.name: Diagonal evaluation
nodes.statement: Partition $\mathbb{N}\times\mathbb{N}$ via the bijection $\mathtt{diagEquiv} : (n,m) \mapsto \text{inl}(n-m,m)$ if $m \le n$, $\text{inr}(m-n-1,n)$ otherwise. The $k$-diagonal $(m \le n, k = n-m)$ sum equals $z^k X^{\binom{k}{2}}$ by Theorem~\ref{thm:fps-cauchy-nonneg}; the $l$-diagonal $(m > n, l = m-n-1)$ sum equals $z^{-(l+1)} X^{\binom{l+2}{2}}$ by Theorem~\ref{thm:fps-cauchy-neg}.
nodes.statement_short: Split via diagEquiv and evaluate diagonals.

nodes.name: Conclude
nodes.statement: Summing over all $k$ and $l$ gives \texttt{jtpSeries}.

nodes.name: Comparison of the FPS and analytic proofs
nodes.statement: The FPS proof (Theorem~\ref{thm:fps-jtp}) works over \emph{any} commutative ring with discrete topology and needs no $\|q\|<1$ hypothesis; the analytic proof (Theorem~\ref{thm:jtp-full}) works in $\mathbb{C}$ with $\|q\| < 1$ and $\|z\| < 1$. \item The analytic proof is extended to all $z\neq 0$ by Theorem~\ref{thm:jtp-analytic}; the FPS proof is already valid for all $z \in A^\times$. \item Both use the same algebraic infrastructure (Sections~\ref{sec:qPochhammer-formalized}--\ref{subsec:qbin-finite-formalized}). The key identity ($S_k = (q;q)_\infty^{-1}$) is proved analytically in Theorem~\ref{thm:S-sum-eq} and algebraically (in $R[\![ X]\!]$) in Theorem~\ref{thm:fps-key}.
nodes.statement_short: FPS proof works over any discrete ring with no norm hypotheses; analytic proof needs $\|q\|<1$; both share the algebraic infrastructure.

nodes.name: Partition and partition function
nodes.statement: A \emph{partition} of a positive integer $n$, also called an integer partition, is a way of writing $n$ as a sum of positive integers. Two sums that differ only in the order of their summands are considered the same partition. The \emph{partition function} $p(n)$ represents the number of possible partitions of a natural number $n$.
nodes.genus: a way of writing $n$ as a sum of positive integers
nodes.label: def:partition

nodes.name: Generating function for partitions
nodes.statement: The generating function for $p(n)$ is given by $$\sum_{n=0}^\infty p(n)\,x^n=\prod_{k=1}^\infty(1+x^k+x^{2k}+\ldots)=\prod_{k=1}^{\infty}(1-x^k)^{-1}.$$
nodes.label: lemma:gen-func-p

nodes.name: Proof of partition generating function
nodes.statement: We work in the ring of formal power series $\mathbb{Z}[[x]]$. \textbf{Step 1.} For each fixed $k \geq 1$, the geometric series identity $$1 + x^k + x^{2k} + \cdots = \sum_{j=0}^\infty x^{jk} = (1 - x^k)^{-1}$$ holds as formal power series. This gives the second equality. \textbf{Step 2.} Expand the product $\prod_{k=1}^\infty (1 + x^k + x^{2k} + \cdots)$. Each term in the expansion is obtained by selecting, for every $k \geq 1$, an exponent $j_k \in \mathbb{Z}_{\geq 0}$ (with $j_k = 0$ for all but finitely many $k$) and multiplying the chosen monomials. Such a selection contributes a single term $$\prod_k x^{j_k \cdot k} = x^{\sum_k j_k \cdot k}.$$ \textbf{Step 3.} The coefficient of $x^n$ is therefore the number of tuples $(j_1, j_2, \ldots)$ with $\sum_k k \cdot j_k = n$. \textbf{Step 4.} Such a tuple corresponds bijectively to a partition of $n$: $j_k$ is the multiplicity of the part $k$. Hence the coefficient of $x^n$ equals $p(n)$, and the first equality follows.
nodes.statement_short: Expand geometric series and biject exponent tuples with partitions by multiplicities.

nodes.name: Partitions of n into distinct parts
nodes.statement: Let $n \in \mathbb{N}$. We define the following sets of partitions of $n$ into distinct positive parts: \begin{align*} \mathcal{P}(n) &= \left\{ S \subseteq \{1, \ldots, n\} \;\middle|\; \sum_{s \in S} s = n \right\}, \\ \mathcal{P}_{\mathrm{even}}(n) &= \left\{ S \in \mathcal{P}(n) \;\middle|\; |S| \equiv 0 \pmod{2} \right\}, \\ \mathcal{P}_{\mathrm{odd}}(n) &= \left\{ S \in \mathcal{P}(n) \;\middle|\; |S| \equiv 1 \pmod{2} \right\}. \end{align*} We further define the number of even and odd partitions of $n$ as $p_e(n) = |\mathcal{P}_{\mathrm{even}}(n)|$ and $p_o(n) = |\mathcal{P}_{\mathrm{odd}}(n)|$.
nodes.statement_short: $\mathcal{P}(n)$: sets of distinct positive parts summing to $n$, split by parity of size; $p_e,p_o$ their counts.
nodes.label: def:distinct-partitions

nodes.name: Expansion of the Euler product
nodes.statement: We have $$\prod_{k=1}^{\infty}(1-x^k)\,=\,\sum_{s=0}^\infty\,\sum_{k_1<k_2<\cdots<k_s}(-1)^s\,x^{k_1+k_2+\ldots+k_s}\,=\,\sum_{n=0}^\infty c_n\, x^n$$ where $c_0=1$ and $c_n=p_e(n)-p_o(n)$ for $n\geq 1$.
nodes.label: lemma:expansion-product

nodes.name: Proof of expansion of the Euler product
nodes.statement: We expand the infinite product as a formal power series. \textbf{Step 1: Expansion as a sum over finite subsets.} For each $k \geq 1$, the factor $(1 - x^k)$ contributes either $1$ or $-x^k$ when expanding the product. A choice across all factors corresponds to a finite subset $$K = \{k_1 < k_2 < \cdots < k_s\} \subseteq \mathbb{Z}_{\geq 1}$$ (the indices for which $-x^k$ was selected). The contribution is $$\prod_{k \in K} (-x^k) = (-1)^{|K|}\, x^{\sum_{k \in K} k} = (-1)^s \, x^{k_1 + \cdots + k_s}.$$ Summing over all such $K$ yields the first equality. \textbf{Step 2: Grouping by total exponent.} A subset $K$ of size $s$ summing to $n$ is exactly a partition $S \in \mathcal{P}(n)$ with $|S| = s$. Hence the coefficient of $x^n$ equals $$c_n = \sum_{S \in \mathcal{P}(n)} (-1)^{|S|}.$$ \textbf{Step 3: $c_0 = 1$.} Only $S = \emptyset$ partitions $0$ into distinct positive parts, contributing $(-1)^0 = 1$. \textbf{Step 4: $c_n = p_e(n) - p_o(n)$ for $n \geq 1$.} Splitting the sum by parity of $|S|$: $$c_n = \sum_{\substack{S \in \mathcal{P}(n) \\ |S| \text{ even}}} 1 \;-\; \sum_{\substack{S \in \mathcal{P}(n) \\ |S| \text{ odd}}} 1 = |\mathcal{P}_{\mathrm{even}}(n)| - |\mathcal{P}_{\mathrm{odd}}(n)| = p_e(n) - p_o(n).$$
nodes.statement_short: Expand the product as a sum over finite subsets and group by total exponent and parity.

nodes.statement: We expand the infinite product as a formal power series.

nodes.name: Proof of Euler's pentagonal number theorem via Franklin's involution
nodes.statement: The proof combines the previous expansion lemma with the closed-form computation of $p_e(n) - p_o(n)$ via Franklin's involution. \textbf{Step 1: Coefficient identification.} By Lemma~\ref{lemma:expansion-product}, $$\prod_{i=1}^\infty (1 - x^i) = \sum_{n=0}^\infty c_n \, x^n,$$ where $c_0 = 1$ and $c_n = p_e(n) - p_o(n)$ for $n \geq 1$. \textbf{Step 2: Closed form for $c_n$.} By Lemma~\ref{lemma:pe-minus-po-closed-form} below, $$p_e(n) - p_o(n) = \begin{cases} (-1)^k & \text{if } n = (3k^2 - k)/2 \text{ for some } k \in \mathbb{Z}_{\geq 1}, \\ (-1)^k & \text{if } n = (3k^2 + k)/2 \text{ for some } k \in \mathbb{Z}_{\geq 1}, \\ 0 & \text{otherwise.} \end{cases}$$ \textbf{Step 3: Reassembling the sum.} The values of $n$ where $c_n \neq 0$ are exactly the (generalized) pentagonal numbers $n = (3k^2 \pm k)/2$ for $k \geq 1$, plus $n = 0$. Each contributes $(-1)^k$. Hence $$\prod_{i=1}^\infty (1 - x^i) = 1 + \sum_{k=1}^\infty (-1)^k \left( x^{(3k^2 - k)/2} + x^{(3k^2 + k)/2} \right).$$ \textbf{Step 4: Bilateral sum reformulation.} Reindex the second family by $k \mapsto -k$. For $k \in \mathbb{Z}_{\geq 1}$, set $k' = -k$, so $k' \in \mathbb{Z}_{\leq -1}$ and $$\frac{3(k')^2 - k'}{2} = \frac{3k^2 + k}{2}, \qquad (-1)^{k} = (-1)^{|k'|} = (-1)^{k'}.$$ The $k = 0$ term gives $(-1)^0 \, x^0 = 1$, matching the leading $1$. Combining the three contributions: $$\sum_{k \in \mathbb{Z}_{\geq 1}} (-1)^k x^{(3k^2 - k)/2} \;+\; (-1)^0 x^0 \;+\; \sum_{k' \in \mathbb{Z}_{\leq -1}} (-1)^{k'} x^{(3(k')^2 - k')/2} \;=\; \sum_{k \in \mathbb{Z}} (-1)^k x^{(3k^2 - k)/2}.$$
nodes.statement_short: Identify coefficients as $p_e(n)-p_o(n)$ and use the closed form from Franklin's involution, then reindex into a bilateral sum.

nodes.name: Base and slope
nodes.statement: Consider a nonempty partition $S \subseteq \{1, \ldots, n\}$ of $n$ into different parts. We define the \emph{base} $b \in S$ as the smallest element of the partition, $b = \min(S)$. Let $\max(S)$ denote the largest element of $S$. We define the \emph{slope} $s$ as: \begin{equation*} s = \max\{k \geq 1 : \max(S), \max(S)-1, \max(S)-2, \ldots, \max(S)-k + 1 \in S\}. \end{equation*} and the \emph{slope set} $D$ as $\{\max(S), \max(S)-1, \ldots, \max(S)-s + 1\}$.
nodes.statement_short: For a partition $S$ into distinct parts: base $b=\min S$, slope $s$ = length of the top consecutive run, slope set $D$ that run.
nodes.label: def:base-slope

nodes.name: Recall criteria
nodes.statement: The empty partition belongs only to $\mathcal{P}_{\mathrm{special}}(0)$ by definition. For nonempty $S \in \mathcal{P}(n)$ with base $b$, slope $s$, slope set $D$, recall the membership criteria: \begin{itemize} \item $S \in \mathcal{P}_\alpha$ iff ($b \leq s$ and $b \notin D$) or $b \leq s - 1$; \item $S \in \mathcal{P}_\beta$ iff ($b > s$ and $b \notin D$) or $b \geq s + 2$; \item $S \in \mathcal{P}_{\mathrm{special}}$ iff $b \in D$ and ($b = s$ or $b = s + 1$). \end{itemize}

nodes.name: Step 1: alpha and beta disjoint
nodes.statement: \textbf{Step 1: $\mathcal{P}_\alpha \cap \mathcal{P}_\beta = \emptyset$.} Suppose $S \in \mathcal{P}_\alpha \cap \mathcal{P}_\beta$. Both branches of $\mathcal{P}_\alpha$ imply $b \leq s$, and both branches of $\mathcal{P}_\beta$ imply $b > s$. Contradiction.

nodes.name: Step 2: alpha and special disjoint
nodes.statement: \textbf{Step 2: $\mathcal{P}_\alpha \cap \mathcal{P}_{\mathrm{special}} = \emptyset$.} Suppose $S \in \mathcal{P}_{\mathrm{special}}$, so $b \in D$ and $b \in \{s, s + 1\}$. \begin{itemize} \item In particular $b \geq s$, so the second clause of $\mathcal{P}_\alpha$ ($b \leq s - 1$) fails. \item The first clause requires $b \notin D$, but $b \in D$, so it also fails. \end{itemize} Hence $S \notin \mathcal{P}_\alpha$.

nodes.name: Assume special
nodes.statement: Suppose $S \in \mathcal{P}_{\mathrm{special}}$, so $b \in D$ and $b \in \{s, s + 1\}$. \begin{itemize}

nodes.name: Second clause fails
nodes.statement: In particular $b \geq s$, so the second clause of $\mathcal{P}_\alpha$ ($b \leq s - 1$) fails.

nodes.name: First clause fails
nodes.statement: The first clause requires $b \notin D$, but $b \in D$, so it also fails. \end{itemize}

nodes.name: Conclude
nodes.statement: Hence $S \notin \mathcal{P}_\alpha$.

nodes.name: Step 3: beta and special disjoint
nodes.statement: \textbf{Step 3: $\mathcal{P}_\beta \cap \mathcal{P}_{\mathrm{special}} = \emptyset$.} Suppose $S \in \mathcal{P}_{\mathrm{special}}$, so $b \in D$ and $b \leq s + 1$. \begin{itemize} \item The second clause of $\mathcal{P}_\beta$ ($b \geq s + 2$) fails since $b \leq s + 1$. \item The first clause requires $b \notin D$, contradicted by $b \in D$. \end{itemize} Hence $S \notin \mathcal{P}_\beta$.

nodes.name: Assume special
nodes.statement: Suppose $S \in \mathcal{P}_{\mathrm{special}}$, so $b \in D$ and $b \leq s + 1$. \begin{itemize}

nodes.name: Second clause fails
nodes.statement: The second clause of $\mathcal{P}_\beta$ ($b \geq s + 2$) fails since $b \leq s + 1$.

nodes.name: First clause fails
nodes.statement: The first clause requires $b \notin D$, contradicted by $b \in D$. \end{itemize}

nodes.name: Conclude
